@@118571624 <h> Scottish university campuses remain powerful engines of enlightenment <p> Edinburgh Futures Institute during the Edinburgh International Book Festival <p> A CAMPUS can be a beautiful and powerful place to be . So all kudos to the Futures Institute ( EFI ) at Edinburgh University . <p> Its campus -- inhabiting the Old Royal Infirmary hospital building -- just won a Special Prize For Interiors in the Prix Versailles , the UN-backed global architecture award . <p> Any of you who swished around the EFI during the International Book Festival this year -- occupying their theatres , teeming cafes and modular hang-out spaces , sweeping up and down dramatic staircases -- will understand this award . <p> In the words of the Prix Versailles judges , " a new public space connects Edinburgh University to the city , unfurling a majestic opening for the benefit of the many " . <p> True -- though the EFI campus , in its flexibility and capacity , is primarily a crucible for multi-disciplinary work and innovation . Many of us will be hoping for extraordinary hybrids and brand-new paradigms to arise from there . <p> Search for " campus " in the news flows of the internet , however , and two aspects immediately rise to the surface . <p> One would be the aspiration that many projects , not just academic , have towards being a " campus " . The other would be the revival of the university campus as a site for protest and resistance . <p> Data centres from Malaysia to Louisiana , by way of a former aluminium smelter in Anglesey , are described in reports this week as " campuses " . Google just launched an " AI campus " for older school students in Camden , London . <p> Many of these plans envision buildings surrounded by trees , parks , public meeting spaces . They summon up the original ideal of the campus -- a congenial space where knowledge is generated . <p> As Wikipedia puts it , the campus tradition begins with medieval European universities , " where the students and teachers lived and worked together in a cloistered environment . " <p> It 's something of a stretch to apply these campus conditions to data centres , with their minimal staffing levels maintaining the infinite whirr of servers . <p> Unless we attribute intellectual power to these enablers of chat-bots and streaming services . <p> Which we should n't ... yet . <p> The term has more pertinence in the big corporate sector -- where locations like the GooglePlex or Apple Park ( below ) in California are rightly titled " campuses " . <p> ( Image : Arne M ? seler ) <p> Indeed , the Silicon Valley ideal is that workers are " cloistered " around their scintillating jobs . The foodbars , the spaces for gaming or chilling out , the sofas for power-napping -- all are intended for you to bring as much of your life-energy to work as possible . <p> ( For a local version of this , look at the promo videos for Barclays ' Glasgow Campus , on the banks of the Clyde . There are quiet rooms for the neurodivergent , fully equipped gyms , compost made in-house for the location 's greenery , crumbly artisanal bakeries ... Why would you ever go home ? ) <p> So there 's a cachet to " campus " that various commercial enterprises seek to invoke -- to my eyes , mostly unjustifiably . <p> As I recall the medieval definition of universities , they were " communities of scholars " . And a " skhole " , in the original Greek etymology , was " the ability to organise your own time , and not learn like a slave " , as Finnish hacker Pekka Himanen once put it . <p> Perhaps you think there 's too much of that " skhole " going around , if you are grumpily disposed towards the current wave of campus radicalism ... <p> Well , tough . We incessantly hear about the career-friendly imperatives of current higher education . However , it seems that gathering young people together to dwell on the bigger ideas , in an easeful and expansive setting , still makes for dissent and rebellion . <p> Thank Socrates for that . <p> Some of the most striking uprisings in history have begun on campuses . Black colleges in the US saw their students protest against Jim Crow laws in the 1910s and 20s . <p> The great uprisings of 1968 in Paris arose from students ' closing down of the University of Nanterre . The Tiananmen Square repression of 1989 was a spillover from campus protests at Peking and Tsinghua universities . <p> Western campuses are currently in upheaval around the massacres of the Israeli state in Gaza . The Columbia University protests this summer were the edgiest , with student occupations of the campus 's central lawn and building being met with violence ( including guns drawn ) from the NYPD . <p> Edinburgh University has also had its share of encampments , hunger strikes and occupations around this issue . <p> ( Image : University of Edinburgh ) <p> The students ' emphasis is on the university 's " severing of research collaborations affiliated with Israel 's genocidal project " ( meaning entities like Leonardo 's , AnyVision , BAE , and Ben-Gurion University ) . <p> The campus as a community of scholars seems to be in full operation at Edinburgh . At the height of events this May , hundreds of university staff signed a letter endorsing all the priority demands of the student protestors around divestment and collaboration . <p> I am generally supportive of student protest . Older generations have pushed the current systems of money and power to the edge of the precipice , in terms of climate breakdown , cost of living , runaway automation , warring geopolitics , the threat of a nuclear exchange . <p> I ca n't blame any young person for putting their training and careers , let alone their bodies and souls , on the line . Again , the possibilities of the campus are there to be seized . <p> What is wrong with trying to assert power from below , over institutions that so often proclaim their ideals to be the highest , yet fall short in the grubbiest ways ? <p> Why should n't kids with the flakiest of futures at least be able ask their elders for moral and ethical consistency ? <p> And who else than students on their campus can establish some distance from the everyday bustle , so they can even perceive the military-industrial complex operating in Scotland ( Angus Robertson failing , in my view , to distance the Scottish Government 's business subsidies from that complex ) ? <p> I do n't discount the tensions here . Of all places , the university campus has to be an engine of truth , verifiability and enlightenment . And represent a genuine diversity of viewpoints and analyses . <p> Decades ago , when Columbia University was gripped with student protests over the Vietnam War in 1968 , the Marxist sociologist Immanuel Wallerstein warned that campuses would be unpropitious for leftist revolution : " The university is and will remain a bastion of the centre ... kept squarely in the centre and in tension with the right because of the strength of the left " . <p> Just as for Edward Said and Noam Chomsky ( below ) , Wallerstein the radical academic saw universities as " a refuge and a point of sortie " meaning an attack from a defended position . <p> Maybe we need more " campuses " , in the richest sense -- ones that combine these two modes . <p> Both as a comfortable , capacious space for discussion , study and prototyping . And as an ethical community whose members dare to exert power over , and seek a different and more just vision for , the institutions around them . As well as beyond them . <p> So it 's lovely to be judged as beautiful by stellar architects such as Daniel Libeskind and David Adjaye . But maybe the true test of a campus comes when , to quote the Prix Versailles judges again , they " unfurl a majestic opening for the benefit of the many " . <h> Why are you making commenting on The National only available to subscribers ? <p> We know there are thousands of National readers who want to debate , argue and go back and forth in the comments section of our stories . That way , all the trolls who post abuse on our website will have to pay if they want to join the debate -- and risk a permanent ban from the account that they subscribe with . <p> The conversation will go back to what it should be about -- people who care passionately about the issues , but disagree constructively on what we should do about them . @@118587924 <p> From facing deadly conflicts and humanitarian crises in Gaza , Lebanon , Ukraine and Sudan , to witnessing the polarisation in societies that followed a record number of elections around the world , women have had to dig deep and find new levels of resilience . <p> BBC 100 Women acknowledges the toll this year has taken on women by celebrating those who -- through their resilience -- are pushing for change , as the world changes around them . The list also remains committed to exploring the impact of the climate emergency , highlighting climate pioneers who work to help their communities tackle its impacts . <h> Culture &amp; Education <h> Plestia Alaqad , Palestinian Territories <p> Journalist and writer <p> Twenty-two-year-old Plestia Alaqad had recently graduated from university when the war in Gaza began . Her memoir based on these reports , Eyes of Gaza , will be published soon . <p> Alaqad is One Young World 's Journalist of the Year 2024 . She has also campaigned for Palestinians at high-profile forums like the World Government Summit . <p> Alaqad left Gaza in November 2023 . She has been awarded a scholarship for a master 's in media studies in Beirut . <h> Hamida Aman , Afghanistan <p> Media and education entrepreneur <p> When Afghan girls were denied access to secondary education by the Taliban , media entrepreneur Hamida Aman decided to launch the Begum Academy , an online space offering free multimedia courses for students who were not able to attend school . <p> In the last year , the educational platform has provided more than 8,500 videos in Dari and Pashto , covering school curricula for grades seven to 12 . <p> The service followed her Radio Begum project , a station made by women and for women , which was created after the Taliban takeover in 2021 . <h> Svetlana Anokhina , Russia <p> Human rights campaigner <p> Svetlana Anokhina has spent years helping victims of domestic violence escape from Russia 's North Caucasus , a Muslim-majority region straddling Eastern Europe and Asia . <p> Along with other volunteers , she founded the Marem project in 2020 . The initiative helps women at risk from Dagestan , Chechnya and other North Caucasus republics organise evacuations and find temporary accommodation , as well as providing them with legal and psychological support . <p> Last year , the authorities opened a criminal investigation against her on charges of discrediting the Russian Armed Forces . <h> Christina Assi , Lebanon <p> Photojournalist <p> Photojournalist Christina Assi grew up in 1990s Lebanon - a time of constant instability in the aftermath of civil war - and this fuelled her drive to document conflict and cover the untold stories of war . <p> Her life took a tragic turn in October 2023 , when she was severely injured in an Israeli strike in southern Lebanon while reporting . <p> The blast killed fellow journalist Issam Abdallah , five other colleagues were wounded and Assi would later have a leg amputated . <p> The experience led her to campaign for journalists ' safety , and she dedicated her participation in the 2024 Olympic torch relay in Paris to all the journalists who have died in the line of duty . <h> Eugenia Bonetti , Italy <p> Nun <p> Sister Eugenia Bonetti has helped manage more than 100 shelters and establish a network with nuns in Africa to support migrant women victims of human trafficking and exploitation . <p> She spent many nights assisting women who had been forced into the sex trade in Rome and became the president of Slaves No More , an organisation that raised awareness of human trafficking . <p> Bonetti was a missionary in Kenya for more than 24 years and helped train officials in various countries to develop anti-trafficking initiatives . <p> Before retiring , she was asked by Pope Francis to write the 2019 Way of the Cross , a key annual devotion for Catholics marking Good Friday at the Colosseum . <h> Shin Daewe , Myanmar <p> Film-maker <p> Award-winning documentary maker Shin Daewe was arrested when found with a drone in her luggage . <p> She was put on trial this year in military-ruled Myanmar , accused of violating counter-terrorism laws . At a closed court , she was denied legal representation and sentenced to life imprisonment . <p> The film-maker has opposed military rule since 1988 and is no stranger to detention . <p> She has directed a dozen short documentaries , many of which have attracted international attention , including her film about the 2007 pro-democracy protests , where thousands of Buddhist monks joined the demonstrations against the junta . <h> Tracey Emin , UK <p> Artist <p> In the 1990s , Tracey Emin rose to prominence for provocative pieces such as My Bed and Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963-1995 , also known as The Tent , which invite people to reflect on their sexual experiences . <p> She has since become an instantly recognisable name in the art world , celebrated for her confessional and autobiographical style . <p> It 's now 25 years since My Bed was first exhibited in London , sparking much media debate . Once portrayed as the enfant terrible of British art , this year Emin has been made a dame for her contributions to the visual arts . <p> The artist has set up the Tracey Emin Foundation in Margate , UK , to nurture upcoming talent . <p> Being a woman right now , I think we need as much resilience as we can have . I think now is a time when there has to be greater unity and a greater fight for women . <p> Tracey Emin <h> Cristina Rivera Garza , Mexico/US <p> Writer <p> Prolific author Cristina Rivera Garza has been recognised with many awards over the years , including the 2024 Pulitzer Prize in the memoir category for her book Liliana 's Invincible Summer , which shines a light on the issue of femicide . <p> Through the story of her sister Liliana -- murdered in 1990s Mexico by a former boyfriend who fled and was never brought to trial -- the writer confronts the trauma of losing a loved-one and embarks on a quest for justice in a country with one of the highest femicide rates in the world . <p> Rivera Garza is also the founder and chair of the PhD programme in creative writing in Spanish at the University of Houston . <p> Messing with language continuously and thoroughly so that language may finally convey women 's side of the story may well lay the foundation for any kind of resilience . <p> Cristina Rivera Garza <h> Linda Dr ? fn Gunnarsd ? ttir , Iceland <p> Women 's shelter manager <p> At the Icelandic Women 's Shelter , Linda Dr ? fn Gunnarsd ? ttir helps those who are forced to leave their homes due to domestic violence . <p> Iceland is a country that often tops the rankings as the " best place to be a woman " , but where gender-based violence rates remain persistently high . <p> As the centre 's general manager , she leads the project to open a new space that would be Iceland 's first purpose-built shelter for women . <p> Gunnarsd ? ttir says that 20 years ago , 64% of women who stayed at the shelter eventually went back to their abusers , but that figure is now down to 11% as a result of improved support and services . <h> Maheder Haileselassie , Ethiopia <p> Photographer <p> Working in a landscape of dried rivers and decimated crops , Ethiopian photographer Maheder Haileselassie documents how severe drought has pushed families in her country to give their daughters up to child marriage . n , Colombia <p> Social activist <p> A visit to a Colombian prison transformed the life of actress Johana Baham ? n , inspiring her to work for those who needed a " second chance " . <p> In 2012 , she shifted her career from acting to advocating prison reform and founded Fundaci ? n Acci ? n Interna , a non-profit organisation that supports Colombia 's prison population and those who have been released . <p> The foundation is reported to have reached more than 150,000 people and 132 detention centres across the country . <p> The social activist was also the promoter of the 2022 Second Opportunities Law , known as the Johana Baham ? n bill , which established economic incentives to strengthen access to employment and training for people after prison . <p> Being resilient goes beyond getting up and moving forward after a difficulty ; it is making the decision to transform it into an opportunity for personal growth . <p> Johana Baham ? n <h> Sharon Kleinbaum , US <p> Rabbi <p> A pioneer within the Jewish community in New York , rabbi Sharon Kleinbaum has spent three decades inspiring change at the intersection of LGBTQ+ rights and religion . <p> Appointed in 1992 as the first female rabbi of the city 's Congregation Beit Simchat Torah , she has led the community through ups and downs - including the Aids crisis in the 1990s . <p> She oversaw an expansion of the congregation 's membership to include trans and non-binary people , and it is now believed to be the largest LGBTQ+ friendly synagogue in the US . <p> Kleinbaum , who retired this year , has been the leading force behind social justice projects and was appointed to the US Commission on International Religious Freedom by President Joe Biden . <p> Joy is an act of spiritual and political resistance . <p> Sharon Kleinbaum <h> Lesley Lokko , Ghana/UK <p> Architect <p> Her work " to democratise architecture " has earned Lesley Lokko the Royal Institute of British Architects ' 2024 gold medal - one of the world 's highest honours in her field - making her the first black woman to receive the award since the institute 's founding in 1848 . <p> She has championed bringing people of under-represented backgrounds into the industry over the past two decades . <p> The Ghanaian-Scottish academic also became the first woman of African descent to curate the Venice Biennale of Architecture , where she focused on the themes of decarbonisation and decolonisation . <p> She is the founder of the African Futures Institute in Accra , which explores the relationship between architecture , identity and race . <p> Resilience is the capacity to stay the course over the long-haul - even in the face of indifference , which is often harder to endure than opposition . <p> Lesley Lokko <h> Olivia McVeigh , UK <p> Make-up artist <p> After being diagnosed with alopecia , Olivia McVeigh began to explore the world of wigs . @@118599083 <p> There is no region where Donald Trump was and is more popular than the Arab world . He speaks a language of power they understand : using military strength and maintaining loyalty to friends . The political oxygen of the region is full of toxic substances spread by two entities : the ( Shia ) revolutionary government of Iran and the ( Sunni ) Muslim Brotherhood , born in Egypt . Hezbollah , Hamas , al-Qaeda , Isis and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham in Syria are all variants of a venom that violates peace and prosperity . <p> From the almost weekly hate marches in London to the anti-Jewish riots on American campuses since the October 7 attacks on Israel , the toxin of political Islamism is protected by the fact that it has now spread far beyond the Middle East . But Trump immediately banning the Muslim Brotherhood and its affiliates in America would force Europe to reconsider the financial , media , and mosque networks used by Iran and the Brotherhood in their own countries to project power back into the Middle East . So a Muslim Brotherhood ban , not a Muslim ban , is needed urgently . <p> A policy shift from Washington under Trump to confront Tehran would also strengthen the West 's allies in the Middle East . Renewed sanctions on the Iranian regime , bold preparedness to destroy its nuclear weapons programme , and the removal or minimisation of its octopus-like imperial tentacles in Yemen , Syria , Lebanon , Gaza , and Iraq would open the pathway to eliminating ideological pollutants and reshaping the region towards greater pluralism and tolerance . <p> Trump possesses the strength of conviction and military power , consolidated by his loyalty to his Arab and Israeli friends , to then build on the signature achievement of his previous presidential term : the Abraham Accords . But Iran and the Muslim Brotherhood have made his job of achieving greater peace and normalisation with Israel more difficult . Israel 's war in Gaza has radicalised millions of young people in Saudi Arabia and the wider region , making the need to see some form of a Palestinian state , guaranteeing Israel 's security and achieving dignity for Palestinians , more urgent . <p> Israeli polling does not show willingness for the creation of a Palestinian state . Palestinian schools and mosques teach a culture of Jew-hatred and killings . This is the deadlock that must be undone . With American security guarantees , Trump could mobilise Arab and Muslim nations to assist in this difficult process . <p> Trump will not persuade more countries to sign up to the Abraham Accords , but other nations could normalise their diplomatic and trade relations with Israel in other ways . Senegal and Morocco already have a peaceful relationship with Israel . Mauritania could be the next candidate for closer ties . It has an outsized influence on global Islamic scholarship , and Trump would find willing partners in the country seeking to normalise relations with Israel . <p> Similarly , in Indonesia , the largest Muslim nation in the world , there are major political parties and leaders willing to reach a rapprochement with the Israelis . Then there is Imran Khan in Pakistan , currently in prison on trumped up charges , but a friend of sorts to Trump and his wife . Could the president-elect call for his release and demand that Pakistan , in return for financial assistance and other help , re-imagine its relationships with Israel ? It would outsmart India , too . <p> Trump 's peacemaker impulse , however , must be encouraged and supported while knowing that within the ranks of his inner circle are influential men and women with dangerously misplaced views . Events could empower the wrong people at the court of King Trump . <p> Indeed , ahead of his January 20 inauguration , the balance of power in the Middle East is already shifting . Israel has weakened Iran , Hamas , and Hezbollah , but the situation in Syria is again becoming dangerous . Assad is a mass murderer , but the Islamist rebels marching towards Damascus will not be any better in government and will provide a new base for Hamas , al-Qaeda , and other enemies of the West . Trump may have to find solace in Trotsky 's warning that " you may not be interested in war , but war is interested in you " . <p> But the broader conditions in the Middle East are conducive to a new approach by the president-elect . The West has partnerships now in the Middle East that are not dominated by the struggles of T E Lawrence , or by Churchill 's handling of Arab nationalists . The political and economic gravity is no longer in Cairo or Baghdad , but in Riyadh , Abu Dhabi , and Doha . These are pro-American cities and countries with which the West can advance common interests in security , trade and innovation . <p> In Abu Dhabi and Riyadh , I hear talk of joint Arab-Israeli space exploration and artificial intelligence-empowered medical advances . In Cairo , I hear talk of Gaza tunnels and terrorism . Trump 's choices are clear . <p> Ed Husain is a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a professor at Georgetown University 's School of Foreign Service

@@118605102 <p> It was not a coincidence that the Syrian group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ( HTS ) began its push for the city of Aleppo on the same day that Israel and Hezbollah agreed a ceasefire to end the fighting in Lebanon . The domino effect set in motion by Hamas on 7 October 2023 is still rippling through the Middle East , this weekend resulting in the spectacular downfall of Syria 's president , Bashar al-Assad . <p> A country that suffered under a Ba'athist regime for 60 years , as well as 14 years of civil war , is celebrating hard-won freedoms as thousands of disappeared people pour out of Assad 's infamous prisons . What comes next in Syria , which still has to grapple with deep internal and sectarian problems , is uncertain . In Iran , though , the picture is clearer : Ayatollah Ali Khamenei can no longer deny that Tehran 's political and military " axis of resistance " has collapsed . <p> Hezbollah , the Shia Lebanese movement long backed by Iran in their shared fight against Israel , miscalculated in coming to Hamas 's aid in the war in Gaza by opening a front on the UN-demarcated blue line that separates the Lebanese from their Israeli neighbours . <p> After almost a year of tit-for-tat cross-border attacks that displaced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes , Israel stepped up its campaign in September . It managed to wipe out much of Hezbollah 's command structure in airstrikes , including its longtime secretary general , Hassan Nasrallah , and drove the group 's fighters away from the demarcation zone in a ground offensive . <p> Two months later , Tehran told Hezbollah it could not afford to take more losses and the group came limping to the negotiation table , agreeing to a ceasefire on terms favourable to Israel . <p> Iran has long needed Hezbollah in neighbouring Syria , too , where the Lebanese group , together with Russian forces , were instrumental in the Assad regime 's survival when it was on the brink of falling to assorted rebel forces in 2015 . But bled dry by the wars with Israel and Ukraine , neither side was willing or able to come to Damascus 's aid this time . <p> Syrian rebels broadcast first news bulletin on state television -- video <p> The Islamist HTS , along with an umbrella of Turkish-backed militias known as the Syrian National Army , sensed a moment of opportunity , gambling that Assad 's allies were weakened and disorganised . They moved on Aleppo , reportedly to stymie a planned regime offensive on their strongholds in north-west Syria , and found that Damascus 's corrupt and demoralised army was caught unawares and offered little resistance . <p> After 14 years of bloodshed that triggered the worst refugee crisis since the second world war , created Islamic State and stoked the flames of populist politics around the world , scenes from around Syria this weekend once again resemble the hopeful early days of the Arab spring protests . <p> There are major geopolitical repercussions for the region and the rest of the world . The crimes committed in the regime 's prisons , now exposed to the light of day , will require robust and internationally coordinated efforts to bring Assad and his lackeys to justice . <p> Assad 's fall effectively severs the weapons , materiel and personnel route from Tehran to Hezbollah , particularly if Syrian Kurdish forces , which have expanded their control of the desert border between Syria and Iraq , remain in position with US backing . Hezbollah , already isolated , will be further weakened , making it more vulnerable to Israeli attack or infiltration . <p> Iran will be forced to double down on its network of proxies in Iraq and its links to the Houthi militia in Yemen , but crucially it no longer has a direct presence or influence on Israel 's borders . It may instead focus on its nuclear programme , but the re-election of Donald Trump -- who orchestrated a " maximum pressure " policy towards Tehran during his first term -- means Khamenei will have to proceed with caution . <p> In the short term , Israel should be delighted with events in Syria , coming as they do on the back of victories over other elements of the axis of resistance -- the decimation of Hezbollah and the near eradication of Hamas in the Gaza Strip -- although they are accompanied by new challenges . <p> The Israel Defense Forces ( IDF ) entered the Syrian-controlled part of the Golan Heights on Saturday for the first time since 1974 to help repel an assault by rebel forces on a UN outpost near the Druze village of Khader , a few hundred metres from Israeli-occupied territory . On Sunday the IDF said two extra brigades had been deployed and troops sent into the buffer zone to keep Islamist rebel groups and potential refugee flows away . <p> Israel is also worried about where the Syrian regime 's heavy weaponry and likely reserves of chemical weapons will end up , as well as potential renewed Iranian efforts to smuggle arms and materiel into the occupied West Bank through Jordan . <p> At this point it is hard to imagine the HTS leader , Abu Mohammed al-Jolani , sitting down to sign a peace deal between Syria and Israel that finally settles the fate of the Golan Heights . But as the past 14 months have proven , nothing in the Middle East is off the table any more .

To Syrians , the message was clear : Assad was gone , and rebels were in control . <p> With the president ousted , the kingdom of silence had suddenly come alive . He led a squadron of fighters who commandeered the broadcast -- reading from a piece of paper as he declared the end of the Assad regime . <p> Now , he was occupied with navigating the city he had just helped capture . He kept getting lost , making U-turns and squinting at Google maps . It was the first time he had been in the capital city in years . <p> Not even the rebels seemed to anticipate having taken Damascus so quickly -- they travelled around the capital city seemingly in a daze . Their guns , which they had been firing just hours before , now sat in the boot of the car untouched . <p> " We did n't want to have to fight for 13 years , we should n't have had to . As a former Alba Party MP candidate , I feel compelled to shed light on the far-reaching consequences of this short-sighted action and call for immediate intervention . <p> The Grangemouth refinery is not merely an industrial site , it is a cornerstone of Scotland 's economy . This single facility supports 2822 jobs across Scotland , with 532 direct employees at the refinery itself . <p> The closure of Grangemouth would be economic suicide . It would make Scotland the only top 25 major oil-producing country in the world without an oil refinery , severely compromising our energy security and industrial capabilities . <p> The refinery 's importance extends far beyond mere numbers . It provides high-quality employment , with average salaries 45% above the local average in Falkirk . The loss of 532 well-paid , technical jobs would be a crushing blow to the local community , potentially triggering a domino effect of economic decline . <p> Moreover , the refinery 's closure would disproportionately affect the local area , with 57% of employees residing in Falkirk and an additional 11% in West Lothian . The resulting unemployment could exacerbate existing areas of deprivation in Grangemouth , leading to increased social challenges and reduced opportunities for our young people . <p> This is not the first time that Grangemouth has faced closure . Former first minister Alex Salmond successfully intervened on two occasions to save Scotland 's only oil refinery , demonstrating the kind of leadership and foresight that is sorely lacking today . <p> The current Westminster and Scottish governments have failed miserably in their duty to protect this vital asset . @@118605344 <p> The fall of President Assad 's regime has been surprisingly swift , coming after many assumed the civil war in Syria ended five years ago -- or even more . <p> However , rebels who were previously pushed back to a small pocket of resistance in northwest Syria , centred on the city of Idlib , have staged a stunning resurgence and taken the main cities of Aleppo , Hama , Homs and Damascus in quick succession . <p> The main rebel force is a jihadist group called Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham , or HTS , who were formed from an affiliate of Al Qaeda . Now the world will be watching how they will establish their dominance in Syria , after Assad has fled . <p> Syria 's rebel-held northern city of Idlib after a strike by the regime 's air force on Sunday <p> MUHAMMAD HAJ KADOUR/AFP/GETTY IMAGES <h> Who are the HTS rebel group ? <p> The name of HTS translates to " Organisation for the Liberation of the Levant " and it remains a sanctioned terrorist group in Britain , the United States and much of the outside world . <p> It was originally known as Jabhat al-Nusra , a Salafist Muslim jihadist group that emerged early in Syria 's civil war in 2012 and was confirmed as Al Qaeda 's affiliate in the conflict the following year , in opposition to Islamic State . <h> Advertisement <p> Led by Abu Mohammad al-Jolani , the so-called " Nusra front " was an aggressive Islamist force committed to replacing Assad 's regime with a Sharia-law-based government in the early years of the war . <p> However in 2016 he publicly split with Ayman al-Zawahiri , Al Qaeda 's leader , and rebranded the group , before merging with other rebel groups to form HTS the following year . <h> Who is their leader ? <p> Jolani , 42 , was born Ahmed Hussein al-Shara in Saudi Arabia , reportedly as the child of Syrian exiles . In the late 1980s , his family moved back to Syria , and in 2003 , he travelled as a radicalised young man to join Al Qaeda in Iraq and fight the US occupation . <p> Like Abu Bakr Al-Baghdadi , the founder of Isis , Jolani spent several years in an American prison in Iraq . At the beginning of the Syrian civil war he returned to fight there , founding Jabhat al-Nusra and taking on his nom de guerre . <h> How does HTS compare to other rebel forces -- and has it lost its jihadist ideology ? <p> Although for a time Isis became far more notorious and successful , HTS survived the fall of its rival 's so-called caliphate , and its independence proved an advantage on the battlefield in northwest Syria . <h> Advertisement <p> Unlike the Syrian Democratic Forces , which is constrained by its US backer ; the regime , which was dependent on Russia and Iran ; and the " mainstream " northern rebels which are tightly controlled by Turkey , HTS could act autonomously . <p> Jolani was also proving a smart and calculating politician . He may have sprung from the same nest as Baghdadi but he realised a more moderate face was necessary if he was to avoid Isis 's fate . <p> He took to wearing western suits and trimmed his beard and hair . He worked with aid agencies to re-establish order and services in Idlib . He opened up to western media , largely ending the longstanding kidnap threat against journalists in Syria . <p> Despite the acrimonious split with Al Qaeda , however , some analysts are not convinced that HTS has wholly renounced its jihadist roots . In Idlib , the group espoused a government guided by a conservative and at times hardline Sunni Islamist ideology . <p> Meanwhile , Jolani was also planning an attack , described initially as defensive , to deter airstrikes and other assaults on his positions by Assad regime troops . It was meticulously timed , with Russia and Hezbollah , the pillars of the regime 's defence , both weakened by their own wars , and the world focusing on Gaza and Lebanon . <h> Advertisement <p> Nir Boms , a professor at the Dayan Center for Middle East studies , said : " Jolani needs to show a degree of pragmatism if he wants to succeed in bringing freedom to Syria . " <p> Jolani has issued a number of statements vowing to unite Syria and , crucially , to protect minorities including Christians , Druze and Kurds . He has promised not to harm the Alawites , who backed Assad . But protests about HTS rule in Idlib , some of which have brought thousands onto the streets in opposition , suggest Jolani may struggle to bring unity . <p> " While he is somewhat open to the pragmatist view , he has n't shown us all his true colours yet , " said Boms . <p> How did the unrest in Syria begin ? <h> What is the background to the offensive ? <p> The Assad regime 's capture of Aleppo in 2016 had appeared to end the threat from the rebel forces -- both pro-western and jihadist -- which had risen against it in 2011 but were by then confined to the region of Idlib . <h> Advertisement <p> Front lines elsewhere stabilised in 2019 when the SDF , the western-backed Kurdish-led militia , overcame the last stand of Isis at Baghouz in Syria 's far east . <p> Syria was divided into four . @@118630710 <p> If you have a daughter or a grand-daughter or a sister , close your eyes and try to picture her in hell . Deep underground , caged , struggling to breathe in the foetid air , unwashed , ragged clothes , a mane of curly hair crawling with lice , in pain from gunshot wounds to her hand and leg , starving , dehydrated , watched over by men who want to rape or murder her and may put a bullet through her head on a whim ; a young woman stripped of everything that makes us human except , perhaps , some irreducible sense of who she was and may yet be again if she is saved . Trying to second-guess members of a death cult makes you paranoid . <p> The summary execution of six young hostages ( including the American Hersh Goldberg-Polin , whose mother Rachel did everything to publicise her son 's plight ) after 11 months in captivity jolted Mandy into a new sense of urgency , I think . She is now getting as much publicity as she can for the daughter who marked her 28th birthday in a tunnel under Gaza in June . <p> " That was a real low point , " Mandy recalls , " It made me feel like , what does it matter if we know Emily was still alive in March , because the six hostages were all alive and then something happened IDF soldiers came too close and they 're dead the next minute . The terrorists could film Emily , like they filmed Hersh , and then say , ' Okay , you 've done your video ' and put a bullet through her head . " <p> The one sliver of hope she has is that Emily is worth more to the terrorists alive than dead . " But they 're not nice , rational people , Allison , they 're psychopathic monsters and they might suddenly think , ' Oh well , we 're losing , let 's just kill them all . ' And that will be a good way to get back at Israel in the same way they raped those women at the Nova festival because rape is a way of destroying your enemy , or so I 've learnt this past year . So if Hamas feel they 're in a corner and they 're not going to get what they want , they 'll just kill them all . So we need a ceasefire now to get as many people out alive as possible , and they would feel that they 're getting something for it , rather than dragging this thing on and on until it 's too late , because they feel they 've lost so much that they 're going to kill them all . " <p> It was 6.30am on October 7 2023 when Mandy Damari woke to the sound of a siren . She lived on her own in a house about two minutes ' walk from her daughter Emily , who had a small place of her own in Kfar Aza 's youth quarter . Mandy 's son also lived nearby with his wife and two small daughters . A sleepy Mandy thought it was just another siren -- occasional rocket attacks were not unknown that close to Gaza although a ceasefire with Hamas had held for a long time -- but padded to her safe room just in case . Then , the alerts on her phone started to go mad . The Kfar Aza WhatsApp group warned residents to stay indoors because there was an infiltration by terrorists . Mandy heard gunshots outside and shouting in Arabic . One text said that the mayor , who lived a couple of doors away , had been murdered . <p> " Emily messaged me to say , ' Do n't go out of the safe room , Mum . ' I said I needed the loo because I had n't been to the bathroom and she was like , ' Mum , this is serious , Do n't leave the safe room , do n't leave it ! ' " <p> Mandy did n't hear from Emily again for over an hour so she sent her a message saying , " Are you asleep ? And Emily replied , ' Are you mad ? I 'm petrified , I 'm not asleep . ' " <p> The night before , Emily had been to a friend 's birthday party and had quite a lot to drink . Afterwards , she dropped by her mum 's house in high spirits and teased her saying , ' You do n't love me when I 'm drunk . ' And there she was sitting on my sofa smiling and winking at her brother , " Mandy recalls . <p> So , that terrible October morning , Mandy sent her a message -- " I love you when you 're drunk " -- because I was sure I was never going to get out of that room alive . And Emily sent me a little heart emoji back at ten past eight . And that was the last message I got from her . " <p> Mandy phoned her brother Rob in Leeds , saying she was calling to say goodbye and asked him to tell their father that she loved him . There was no electricity and Mandy was in the dark , her phone soon out of charge . She used the safe room to take private English lessons after kindergarten finished so she came across one of the mini torches she gave as a prize to her students and turned it on sparingly to preserve the batteries . She also found a small bottle of Rescue Remedy , spraying a couple of drops on herself every hour . <p> Mandy could n't see anything , but she heard a burst of gunfire out the front . What she did n't know is that terrorists shot at her front door and somehow a bullet jammed the lock , probably saving her life . Eventually , at about six o'clock in the evening , she heard Israeli voices and became one of the first to be rescued . At a local petrol station , she was reunited with her son and family . No one seemed to know what had happened to Emily , although someone reported that nobody dared attempt a rescue because her area was over-run with terrorists . <p> I walked through the youth quarter on my visit in September ; it looked like the charred aftermath of an apocalypse . All the small , single-storey houses were destroyed . Almost all of Emily 's twentysomething neighbours were murdered , save one who hid behind a mattress and the twins Ziv and Gali Berman who were also taken hostage . <p> At first , Mandy assumed her daughter was fine . " Well , she must have escaped . It 's Emily . There 's no way she 's going to die . " <p> Why did you think that ? <p> " Because it 's Emily . She 's resourceful , she never takes no for an answer , optimistic things will work out as they always do when Emily 's there . " Mum and daughter had been to an Ed Sheeran concert in London the previous year and " she managed to get us inside this golden ring somehow . Blagged her way in . I 'm such a pessimist I always think we 'll never find a parking space and Emily laughs , ' Do n't stress , we 're gon na get one , Mum , ' and it 's there . She seems to make her own luck which is why I have hope that she 's still alive . Because she does know how to survive . " <p> As the days went by and there was no news , Mandy started to believe Emily had been murdered , that they would identify her body at the Shura army base which had become a giant improvised morgue processing the mutilated corpses of scores of girls Emily 's age . <p> It was 11 intolerable days before the Damaris got a message from the Israeli government saying they suspected Emily had been taken hostage ; a week later they confirmed she was in Gaza . <p> Mandy was torn between relief and fear . " My mind was saying , would n't it have been better for her to be murdered and not taken hostage because she 's going to get raped or attacked by Hamas because they were mad in what they did on the seventh of October . " <p> Mandy got no more information until the November ceasefire when she was told that Emily was on a list of women and children who were scheduled for release . <p> This news gave hope to others on the kibbutz , too . In total , 19 people from Kfar Aza were taken hostage and 12 came back - women and children - in that November deal . Emily was not among them , but several had been with her in Gaza and were able to tell Mandy how she was . <p> Hungry for every scrap of knowledge about her child , Mandy has managed to piece together a rough picture of Emily 's life in captivity . " At first , they were kept in a house and they were optimistic . They thought they were going to get released and there was no way Israel would leave hostages in Gaza . Then , the bombing started and the group Emily was with nearly died because a bomb went off very close to where they were staying . But they survived . I told you she 's lucky ! " <p> Mandy learned of her daughter 's injuries -- gunshot wounds to one hand and a leg sustained when Hamas snatched her , also shooting and killing Emily 's beloved cockapoo Choocha . <p> Emily with her mother <p> " They said she was n't getting treated for her injuries , just a bit of pain relief and some out-of-date iodine apparently , and for the first few days she was totally out of it . Then she recovered and started taking care of everyone . This young girl told me that every day Emily used to wake up and start singing , ' It 's a great morning . ' It 's a really terrible song , but it was like an ironic thing , and she got them all singing along . " Emily talked a lot to the older children too , trying to reassure them . <p> Mandy was not surprised to learn her daughter became a go-between between the guards and the hostages . " Another good character trait is that she knows how to get on with anyone in any situation ; she 'll know how to deal with them . Emily took care to be very respectful with their captors : every time she would step out of the room to go to the bathroom she 'd make sure she put on a hijab and covered herself up . She knew how to get on well with the guards , so that they liked her , I suppose . " <p> Mandy suspects Emily must have met girls in Gaza who had been sexually assaulted because one released hostage recalled a conversation Emily had with a guard in which she said to him , " You know what has happened to these women ? You know this is not your religion -- why are you doing it ? " <p> Mandy says she does n't know what the guard replied but it shows " she was n't afraid of them " . <p> So far in the interview , I have tried to be detached and keep my feelings in check -- Mandy 's are the only emotions that matter in this room -- but my own daughter is just five months older than Emily and I am suddenly moved beyond words . Just imagine the courage and the spirit it took for Emily Damari to reprimand a terrorist like that . <p> " You should be very proud of her , " I say and Mandy nods . " She 's very special , you know , she 's an amazing character , which is why she has so many friends . " <p> Later eyewitness reports , dating from when Emily and other hostages had been moved below ground into the vast network of tunnels , were less positive . " They said she had lice and she was constantly scratching , her hair , her body and everywhere . There was only cold water to wash in and a bucket to go to the toilet . No privacy . They wore the same clothes that they 'd had on for the last month and a half , put them back on when they were wet , which is why they got rashes . They were sleeping on thin mattresses that were really smelly and horrible . " <p> As well as enduring her own personal nightmare , Mandy has been living with the wider grief suffered by her community . About 800 people lived on the kibbutz : as a kindergarten teacher , Mandy knew all the parents and children . She went to 64 funerals of friends and neighbours in the first few weeks after October 7 , when she still did n't know the fate of her own child . People wondered aloud how she had the strength , but she says she found it oddly comforting to lose herself in something other than worrying about Emily . <p> She tells me she received proof that Emily was alive at the start of this year and another " proof of life " a few months ago . ( Mandy seems reluctant to say more lest she give something away . ) " Quite a few months ago now , so it 's totally useless because they would n't say how Emily was , if she was walking , if she was eating , it was just she 's alive , that 's it . And it does n't make any difference because you can say she was alive five minutes ago , and in the next five minutes she could be murdered . " <p> Mums are hard-wired to fret about tiny things that will improve their children 's lives , stuff that will give them any slight advantage , and Mandy 's brain continues to do so . Even though she ca n't see Emily or ask her how she is , she clearly obsesses over her situation . When they recovered Hersh Goldberg-Polin 's body from a tunnel , his spine was curved , Mandy says . " Hersh was tall , but Emily is short like me , maybe a bit taller , five feet three , which is good , so perhaps she can stand up in the tunnel ? " Her daughter may be held in some dark stinking airless poky hole , but at least she wo n't have to stoop the whole time -- something to cling to at least . <p> Does she think about what kind of state she 'll be in if she 's released ? <p> " Of course , I mean even for a strong person like Emily it 's going to be a lot . The conditions there are dreadful physically and mentally , well , it 's mental terror , is n't it ? It 's not like they 're in jail . They are in danger every second of their life . So what kind of toll is that taking on her brain ? You know , I was in my safe room for 12 hours with the terrorists outside , and I thought , ' That 's it . I 'm going to die . ' And I 've got a blackout from that period , I ca n't remember much at all . What is it like for Emily after 425 days of that type of terror , every single day ? " <p> Mandy tells me that when Israeli soldiers recovered the body of another young female hostage , Eden Yerushalmi , Hamas had starved her so she weighed 79 pounds -- 22 pounds less than before her abduction . " I mean , Emily was thin to begin with . She used to go running all the time so at least she 's very fit , so maybe she 'd be okay . But the hostages were getting like half a pitta bread and a date to eat . They were n't getting enough food definitely . So she 's probably starving . " <p> Unbidden , a thought comes to my mind of the Jews who survived the concentration camps and Mandy seems to read my mind . " They came out of Auschwitz and they looked like skeletons . So it does n't matter what Emily looks like . Well , it does matter . But , I mean , as long as she 's alive , that 's , you know , that 's the hope -- that she 's alive . " <p> I ask Mandy how she is doing and she shrugs ; indifferent , she clearly could n't care less how she is . " People say , you go and have massages , go to a psychologist . I wo n't do it until Emily 's back , because I 've got no time to sit with these people . I 've got no patience . If anyone talks to me for more than half an hour my concentration wanders . " All she will say is that she is not suffering from PTSD , because she is not " post " the " traumatic stress " . Rather , like Emily 's captivity , it feels neverending . <p> Mandy says she thinks she 'd know if Emily was dead : ' I look for signs . Sounds stupid , I know . Yesterday , I grabbed something to eat . And I was looking at the crisps , and they were called Emily crisps ' Credit : Heathcliff O'Malley <p> A social worker does check in with her once a week and she has a shared bond with parents of other hostages -- Talia Berman , mother of the twins Ziv and Gali ; Aviva Siegel , who was released from Gaza but whose American husband Keith is still there . " She 's a very good friend because she speaks English and she worked with me in the kindergarten . " Mandy gets huge comfort from her friendship with Simona Steinbrecher who knows exactly what she 's going through because her 31-year-old daughter Doron is also a hostage in Gaza . <p> The hostage relatives have a meeting once a week and , occasionally , Mandy goes to the hostage forum in Tel Aviv , although she dislikes the way the hostage cause has become politicised and turned against the Government . " Hamas are to blame , nobody else . " Emily is one of a hundred hostages remaining in the tunnels under Gaza , although not all are alive . <p> Her daughter is her last thought before falling asleep and her first thought on waking . She has a big photo of Emily next to her bed . <p> Do you talk to her ? " Yes , in the morning . I say , ' Keep strong and keep alive . You know I love you . Send you a hug , a virtual hug . Just send me a sign that you 're alive . ' " <p> Mandy thinks that she 'd know if Emily was dead . Although she 's not religious , she says she has a spiritual side . " I look for signs . Sounds stupid , I know , but I do get them occasionally . " Yesterday , she went for a coffee before a TV appearance and grabbed something to eat . And I was looking at the crisps , and they were called Emily crisps . Have you ever heard of crisps called Emily ? And there 's all sorts of weird things like that . " <p> Towards the end , with dusk falling , she tells me perhaps the cruellest thing of all . " Emily thinks I 'm dead . The released hostages told me that she thinks I 'm dead and her brother 's dead because Hamas told her there 's nothing left of your kibbutz , and there 's no one left alive . " Maybe Mandy does interviews like this one and speaks out hoping somehow that someone tells Emily that her mother is fighting for her . My God is she fighting for her . I ca n't believe that a love so fierce and devoted is n't felt by her child . <p> There are reports that Israel is willing to negotiate a ceasefire for the " release of all surviving women , all living men over the age of 50 who are held captive and hostages in serious medical condition " . The name Emily Damari is on the list .

@@118631176 <p> Hello . It looks like you 're using an ad blocker that may prevent our website from working properly . To receive the best experience possible , please make sure any ad blockers are switched off , or add https : **25;2447;TOOLONG to your trusted sites , and refresh the page . <h> Putin braces for Syria 's shockwaves <p> People celebrate atop a toppled statue of Syria 's former president Hafez al-Assad in Damascus on December 8 . Islamist-led rebels took Syrica 's capital in a lightning offensive , sending President Bashar al-Assad fleeing and ending five decades of Baath rule in Syria . Photo by Louai Beshara/ AFP <p> The advance of the Syrian opposition rebels led by the Islamist group , Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ( HTS ) , over the last week explosively reawakened the dormant Syrian civil war . Their success inspired ordinary Syrians living across the country to take the streets and proclaim the end of the brutal dictatorship that began in 1971 when Hafez al-Assad took over the presidency of Syria and ended sometime over the weekend when his son , Bashir al-Assad , fled the country . <p> Images of long-suppressed people pulling down statues of a dictator are greeted with enthusiasm in the West , but the situation in Syria is complex . HTS grew out of the Al-Nusra Front ( Al-Qaeda 's ( AQ ) official affiliate in Syria ) . Its leader , Abu Mohammed al-Jolani fought in the Iraqi insurgency against the US as a member of the group that eventually became Islamic State ( ISIS ) . <p> Other forces operating in Syria include Turkish-backed rebels supported by the Turkish military , Kurdish forces -- including the US-backed People 's Defence Units instrumental in defeating ISIS -- and Syrian government forces supported by Russia and Iranian proxies . It is the only country in the world to have both a US base ( al-Tanf ) and Russian military bases . <p> The consequences of the reignition of this conflict will reverberate outwards from Aleppo , Hama , Homs and Damascus , impacting countless Syrians on the ground , competing ideological and ethnic groups across the region and Bashir al-Assad 's key ally , Vladimir Putin , thousands of miles away in the Kremlin . As well as losing face , Putin has lost Russian military personnel and equipment as well as revenue streams for his war in Ukraine . <p> The civil war began in 2011 as a popular uprising during the wider Arab Spring protests . Assad set his brutal Baathist secret police in motion to crack down on the protestors , prompting the formation of armed rebel groups such as the Free Syrian Army . By mid-2012 , an insurgency had escalated into a civil war . A counter-terrorism ally of the West became an international pariah , allowing Putin to re-establish strong relations between Russia and Syria . <p> Over the next two years insurgent forces , receiving arms from Nato and Gulf Cooperation Council states , made significant advances against the government forces . In 2014 Iran launched a major intervention to support Assad . Russia followed in 2015 . <p> This turned the tide of the conflict . Russia 's intervention primarily consisted of intensive air and missile strikes , but also , in support of the ground offensive by Iranian forces ( including their proxy Hezbollah ) , Putin deployed the private military company Wagner . <p> Wagner 's actions included the 2018 Battle of Khasham , when , alongside Syrian militia , they tried to seize control of an oil field from the US army and allied militias . A priority of the group was to seize control of oil and gas reserves and through a series of Russian companies extract the profits from them , making themselves rich and helping fund Putin 's wars . <p> Their greed was what got them kicked out of Syria when the need for them on the battlefield appeared to have receded . Some of the funding streams they established remained . <p> Syria thanked Russia for their support by being the only Middle Eastern country to vote against the UN General Assembly Resolution , denouncing the Russian invasion of Ukraine . <p> Before launching this offensive , opposition forces will have banked on Russian forces , which have been scaled back from 2015 levels due to redeployments to Ukraine , being unable to ramp back up as easily . They will have assumed the losses of proxies , Hamas and Hezbollah , in Gaza and Lebanon , meant Iran would also be unable to provide the same support as previously . <p> Even though they have professionalised as a military force and are leveraging drone technology , the opposition would not have expected government forces to capitulate so quickly . The garrisons in the north turned out to be hollowed out by corruption and undermined by under-manning . <p> Aleppo , the first city to fall , was held by the rebels between 2012 and 2016 . It was during its siege that Assad dropped chemical weapons , crossing western red lines to no real consequence . Russian and Syrian air forces dropped cluster munitions on populated areas and carried out " double tap " airstrikes to target responding rescue workers . The siege left over 31,000 people dead . It was retaken with ease and the opposition continued towards Hama . <p> Hama also has symbolic significance . On a visit to Syria in early 2001 , US congressmen received a lecture from Assad on how to combat terrorism . " Join the approach that has long been charted by Syria , " he suggested . <p> He was alluding to the flattening of Hama by Syrian tanks in 1982 in an operation by security forces serving Bashir 's father and predecessor , Hafez al-Assad , that killed 25,000 people and destroyed the Syrian Islamist movement led by the Muslim Brotherhood . It has remained a city opposed to Assad 's rule . As Hama fell , Assad raised his soldiers ' salary by 50% . <p> Homs was more strategically important . It sits at the crossroad that leads west to the heartland of Assad 's support , east to the sea and Tartus , the Russian Navy 's only operational base in the Mediterranean , and south towards Damascus . Its impending fall convinced Syrians across the country of Assad 's vulnerability and became the tipping point . <p> Assad pulled his forces back to protect the capital , but even the more well-equipped and well-prepared government forces , such as the Republican Guard , melted away . In war momentum and morale are key and the opposition had both , the government forces had neither . <p> Assad hoped that the calvary would arrive as it did in 2015 . Iran looked to send reinforcements , but realised they were not going to be enough so instead started pulling out its forces . <p> Putin dithered , before initiating a panicked withdrawal of his military and advised all Russian citizens to leave . @@118637156 <h> Shaken by Assad 's sudden fall , Syria faces seismic turning point <p> Syrians may be celebrating the fall of Assad , but the country 's future is uncertain <p> Jeremy Bowen <p> International editor <p> Published <p> 43 minutes ago <p> In the end the Assad regime was so hollow , corrupt and decayed that it collapsed in less than a fortnight . <p> No one I have spoken to has been anything other than astonished by the speed with which the regime turned to dust . <p> In the spring of 2011 , the year of the Arab uprisings , it was different , when Syrians tried to grab some of the revolutionary magic that had swept away the presidents of Tunisia and Egypt and was threatening the veteran strongmen of Libya and Yemen . <p> By 2011 , the regime created by Hafez al-Assad and passed to his son Bashar on his death in 2000 was already corrupt and decadent . <p> But the system that Hafez built still had much of the brutal , ruthless strength that he believed was necessary to control Syria . Assad senior had seized power in a country that was prone to coups and delivered it to his son and heir without a significant challenge . <p> Bashar al-Assad went back to his father 's playbook in 2011 . <p> It is hard to imagine now , but back then he had more legitimacy among some of Syria 's population than the old dictators swept away by crowds chanting the slogan of that year - " The people want the fall of the regime " . <p> Bashar al-Assad was a vocal supporter of the Palestinians and of Hezbollah during its successful fight against Israel in the 2006 Lebanon war . He was younger than the ex and soon to be former Arab leaders . <p> Since his father 's death he had been promising reform . Some Syrians still wanted to believe him in 2011 , hoping demonstrations were the spur he needed for the change that he had promised , until he ordered his men to shoot peaceful demonstrators dead in the streets . <p> A British ambassador in Syria once told me that the way to understand the Assad regime was to watch Mafia films like The Godfather . The obedient could be rewarded . <p> Anyone who went against the head of the family or his closest lieutenants would be eliminated . In Syria 's case that could mean the gallows , or a firing squad , or indefinite incarceration in some underground cell . <p> We 're seeing them now , emaciated and pale , blinking into the light , filmed on the mobiles of the rebel fighters who have freed thousands of them from years behind bars . <p> The weakness of the regime , to the point that it collapsed like a soggy paper bag , was disguised by the fearsome and repressive gulag it still maintained . <p> The international consensus was that Bashar al-Assad was weak , dependent on Russia and Iran , and presiding over a country he had fractured to preserve his family 's rule -- but still strong enough to be regarded as a fact of Middle Eastern life , who could even be useful . <p> In the last days before rebels burst out of Idlib , it was widely reported that the US , Israel and the United Arab Emirates were trying to detach Assad 's Syria from Iran . <p> Israel had been launching increasingly heavy airstrikes against targets inside Syria it said were part of the supply chain Iran used to get weapons to Hezbollah in Lebanon . <p> Israel 's offensive in Lebanon had dealt severe blows to Hezbollah , but the idea was to stop it regenerating . At the same time the UAE and the US were trying to find incentives for him to break the alliance with Tehran , relaxing sanctions and allowing Assad to continue his international rehabilitation . <p> Both Benjamin Netanyahu and Joe Biden have claimed credit for the fall of the Assad regime . There is something in that . <p> The damage Israel inflicted on Hezbollah and Iran with US weapons and constant support , and Biden 's supply of arms for Ukraine , made it impossible , even undesirable , for Assad 's closest allies to save him . <p> But the fact that they saw Assad as part of their strategy to contain and damage Iran until days before his fall indicates clearly that they did not for a moment believe him to be days away from a midnight flit to Russia . <p> They did contribute to his end , more by accident than design . <p> Image source , Getty Images <p> Image caption , <p> The change of regime in Syria has seen many released from the country 's prisons <p> The fall of the regime might have ended Iran 's supply chain , if Syria 's new rulers decide their deals with others are more useful than the Iranian alliance . <p> All sides are thinking hard and thinking again about what comes next , and it is too soon to draw definite conclusions . Syrians , their neighbours , and the wider world are now confronted by another geopolitical earthquake , the biggest of the series that has followed the Hamas attacks on Israel in October last year . It might not be the last . <p> Iran is seeing the final collapse of the main planks of the network it called the axis of resistance . Its most important components have been transformed ; Hezbollah badly damaged and the Assad regime gone . <p> Iran 's rulers might want to follow up on hints of talks on a deal with Donald Trump once he takes office . Or its new strategic nakedness might push it into a fateful decision to turn its highly enriched uranium into a nuclear weapon . <p> Syrians have every reason to rejoice . In the years after 2011 , for all the repression and brutality of the regime , Assad and his acolytes could still find men who would fight . Many of the troops I met on front lines told me that Assad was a better option than the jihadist extremists of Islamic State group . <p> In 2024 , faced by a well-organised rebel force that insisted it was nationalist , Islamist but no longer jihadist , the army 's reluctant conscripts refused to fight , stripped off their uniforms and went home . <p> Image source , EPA <p> Image caption , <p> Syrian troops abandoned military hardware , including tanks , and discarded their uniforms in some cases <p> The best scenario is that Syrians , helped by the big players in the region , will find a way to create a postwar mood of national reconciliation , not a wave of looting and revenge that will drag the country into a new war . Abu Mohammad al Joulani , the leader of victorious HTS , has called for his men and all of Syria 's sects to respect each other . <p> His men have removed the regime , and he is the closest Syria has to a de facto leader . <p> Syria , though , has dozens of armed groups that do not necessarily agree with him and will want to grab power in their own areas . In southern Syria , tribal militias did not recognise the writ of the Assads . They will not follow orders they do n't like from the new set up in Damascus . <p> In the eastern desert , the US saw a big enough threat from remnants of the Islamic State group to launch waves of air strikes . The Israelis , alarmed by the prospect of an Islamist state on their border , are pounding the military infrastructure of Syria 's armed forces . <p> It might be better to find a way to make a reformed Syrian Arab Army part of the solution in a country without much law or order . The reckless decision by the US in 2003 to dissolve the Iraqi armed forces had disastrous consequences . <p> In Turkey , President Erdogan must be satisfied by what he sees . <p> Erdogan 's Turkey did more than any other power to preserve the autonomy of Idlib province , where HTS was transforming itself into a fighting force when Syria seemed to be in the deep freeze . <p> Erdogan might see his influence lapping Israel 's borders , at a time when Israel-Turkey relations have been poisoned by the war in Gaza . <p> The worst scenario for Syrians is that their country will follow the example of two Arab dictatorships that spun into violent chaos after the fall of their regimes . <p> Colonel Gaddafi of Libya and Saddam Hussein of Iraq were removed without a ready-made replacement waiting in the wings . Ill-considered foreign intervention did much to create two catastrophes . <p> The vacuum left by the dictators was filled by waves of looting , revenge , power grabs and civil war . <p> Syrians have not been in charge of their own destiny for generations . Individuals were robbed of it by the two Assad presidents and their followers . The country lost it after war left it so weakened that bigger foreign powers used it to increase and preserve their own power . <p> Syrians still do not have agency over their lives . They might have a chance of creating a new and better country if they did .

@@118638577 <p> In June 2021 , just five months into her stint as Estonian prime minister , Kaja Kallas walked into the headquarters of the European Council to confront Europe 's most powerful leader . <p> As media headlines warned of Russian troops massing on the border of Ukraine , then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel wanted to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to an upcoming summit of European Union leaders in Brussels . <p> The idea had the backing of French President Emmanuel Macron , and Merkel intended to push it through during a meeting of the European Council in Brussels . <p> Advertisement <p> Kallas was n't having it . <p> " A summit on what ? " repeated Kallas , who could count on the support of several other Eastern European countries . <p> Merkel , unable to pull off her plan without at least the grudging consent of her fellow leaders , backed down . <p> As the German chancellor left the room , Macron was in disbelief that a new leader from a small EU country had dared humiliate Merkel , at that time the bloc 's main power player . <p> According to one diplomat , the French president turned to Kallas and , hinting she might face backlash , asked : " Will you still be prime minister tomorrow ? Not only is she taking office during a period of historic geopolitical upheaval , but the job itself is one in which her predecessors have struggled to make a mark . <p> Her portfolio will require her to balance the interests of the EU 's 27 countries , each of which has traditionally enjoyed a veto on matters of foreign affairs . With a reputation as one of Europe 's fiercest Russia hawks , Kallas -- who declined to be interviewed for this article -- will have to overcome the widespread preconception that she 'll be a single-issue foreign policy chief . <p> For Kallas , the job appears to be coming at exactly the right time . Carl Court/Getty Images <p> " If you ask Kallas where Africa is , she might tell you it 's south of Russia , " quipped a senior European diplomat earlier this year . <p> The Estonian firebrand has one important advantage , however : Expectations are low .
