@@119264728 <h> ' Bad things can happen ' : how will the world adjust to the Trump presidency ? <p> Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor <p> 25 December 2024 at 7:00 am*13-min read <p> Donald Trump at an event in Phoenix , Arizona on 22 December.Photograph : Cheney Orr/Reuters <p> " A revisionist state has arrived on the scene to contest the liberal international order , and it is not Russia or China , it is the United States . It is Trump in the Oval Office , the beating heart of the free world . The incoming administration contests every element of the liberal international order -- trade , alliances , migration , multilateralism , democratic solidarity and human rights . <p> " The narrative now at home and abroad is that the US is not what we thought it was . Trump was not an aberration , not a bug , but a feature of American politics and of America 's story . " <p> This stark assessment of the impact of Donald Trump 's return to the White House in January , by the Princeton University professor of politics John Ikenberry , leads him to a question : " Will the new global order be determined less by the US and more by its legacy partners ? Will they seek an alternative framework globally and regionally , or will they make bets to ride this out , and do the transactional politics that Trump is going to request ? " <p> Already , from Ankara to Brussels to Tehran and Moscow , the whole world seems catalysed and in motion as countries seek answers to versions of that question . Without Trump taking a single executive decision , they are positioning , responding and adjusting to the long shadow he represents . Even Trump himself seems a little unnerved at what his return is unleashing . " The world seems to be going a little crazy now , " he recently admitted in Paris . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> Amid the craziness , three distinct forms of response to Trump are starting to emerge . <p> An " ideologically aligned " group is emboldened , including populists in Europe , Latin America and Israel who believe their often Russia-friendly brand of nationalism will benefit from being in the slipstream of America First . The breakup of the European Union , an Argentina-style chainsaw taken to regulation , a new security architecture with Russia , regime change in Tehran : all become possibilities . <p> A second group , led by China , foresees a diplomatic shake-up in which America becomes an agent of instability , leading to some kind of globalised realignment . For Beijing -- facing the threat of 50% tariffs -- the silver lining is that Trump 's willingness to treat friends as foes may create a leadership vacuum that China , as the so-called advocate of " the global majority " , can exploit . <p> It is one version of the " alternative framework " of which Ikenberry speaks . Trump seems aware of that risk and is already threatening to impose 100% tariffs on the Brics countries -- Brazil , Russia , India , China , South Africa , Iran , Egypt , Ethiopia , and the United Arab Emirates -- if they try to replace the US dollar with another currency . <p> The third , more phlegmatic , group is made up of America 's " legacy partners " in Europe and the G7 group of liberal democracies . They still hope that with the right mix of argument , flattery and self-abnegation they can make a rational case that appeals to Trump 's self-interest . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> Leaders of these nominal allies , however much they revile Trump 's methods , look at American power and feel they have no choice but to interact with him . " We have to dance with whoever is on the dancefloor , " Mark Rutte , the new Nato chief , said in February . The battle then becomes one for Trump 's brain , and to persuade him that America 's interests do not stop at its borders . But if this strategy does not work , insurance is being taken out by strengthening alternative frameworks . Polling published this month by the European Council on Foreign Relations , for instance , showed that right across Europe voters prefer more Europe to more Trump . <p> That need not be surprising . Trump , it should be recalled , describes the EU as a " not-so-mini-China " . His threat to impose tariffs has already stimulated an internal debate in Europe on how to respond . The president of the European Central Bank , Christine Lagarde , has been accused of running up the white flag by saying Europe should try to ward off tariffs by buying US arms and liquefied natural gas . <p> The former WTO director general Pascal Lamy described her strategy to " calm this barking dog " as " absolutely wrong " . He said : " You never negotiate with the US , whatever the president , from a position of weakness . We must be strong by showing the importance of our market to US exporters . " <p> But even he admits this will be testing since different countries have different levels of dependence on the US . " Our strength is the size of our market and our unity . Our weakness is our lack of geostrategic consistency and our disunity . " <h> Ukraine <p> Trump 's true existential threat to Europe lies in Ukraine . Without having revealed a detailed peace plan , Trump seems to want to threaten both sides -- Vladimir Putin with rearmament in Ukraine , Volodymyr Zelenskyy with withdrawal of support -- to force an end to the war . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> Asked recently if he was concerned about Trump 's intentions , the outgoing head of the EU 's foreign service , Josep Borrell , said : " How could I not be worried ? Certainly I am . This is the big elephant in the room ; this is the question . What will Europeans do if the new American administration is no longer supporting Ukraine ? This is the question the Ukrainians were asking me when I was visiting Kyiv . It came from the last soldier to the president of Ukraine . I do n't think anyone knows the answer . " <p> Trump complained : " We are in for $350bn . Europe is in for $150bn . That needs to be equalised . The war with Russia is important for everyone , but it 's more important for Europe than us . We have a little thing called an ocean between us . " <p> Faced by the risk Trump will agree a deal with Putin over his head , Zelenskyy at the end of November took pre-emptive action . He proposed a ceasefire in which Ukraine would solely rely on diplomacy -- not armed conflict -- to regain the territory lost to Russia in the east since 2014 , but in return the remaining part of Ukraine would be offered Nato membership , and not just the " well-lit bridge " to membership at some point in the future . <p> But Rutte has already rejected his plan , arguing that none of the key players , including Russia or the US , would accept Ukrainian membership of Nato now . Nato membership includes the key commitment that an attack on one member is an attack on all . <p> That leaves Europe facing some fateful decisions and not much time in which to take them . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> Norbert R ? ttgen , the German CDU foreign affairs specialist , said : " Europe squandered the time it should have spent investing more heavily into the relationship with the US -- including by building up its own defences ... European leaders can not simply shift the blame for their predicament to Washington . " <p> Borrell insists he did try to make Europe learn to speak " the language of power " , and so be capable of acting more independently from the US . This required not just an increase in European defence spending , but a change in mindset that he admits has only just started . He recalls when he was asked how Europe would respond to the Russian attack on Ukraine in 2022 , he instructed his officials to work up an option , and they came up with a plan to spend ? 50m ( ? 41m ) . " I said " Are you crazy ? Put three 0s behind that . We are talking about a real war with bombs falling inside a European city . ' " <p> The use of the European peace facility -- an EU military aid fund -- to help Ukraine , which was advocated by Borrell , was a significant step . Overall progress towards creating a European defence capability has been glacial , however . He blames a lack of political will , symbolised by the opposition within the EU to ending the national veto in all foreign policy decisions . Borrell explained : " We live in an ecosystem where you can not speak , you can not open your mouth if there is no unity . How many times did I have to say ' there is no European position on this ' ? Everyone wants to keep their right to a veto , that is the reality . " <p> Borrell also found Europe 's industrial defence base hollowed out . " I have been begging for arms . It took three months just to ask for 1m rounds of ammunition . Russia is shooting 800,000 in a month . " Since the Ukraine war started , he said , nearly 45% of all the equipment provided by EU nations came from outside the bloc . <p> So a European plan to protect Ukraine is still needed , but Trump is having a galvanising impact . <p> A statement issued earlier this month by foreign ministers from Germany , France , Poland , Italy and the UK after a meeting in Berlin contained a warning to Trump not to strike a deal with Putin behind Europe 's back : " There can be no negotiations about peace in Ukraine without Ukrainians and without Europeans by their side . " <p> The question is , given the shortfalls described by Borrell : can Europe realistically fill the gap if Trump ends US support ? The plan is a European coalition of the willing , cooperating outside EU structures , providing security guarantees to Ukraine by stationing peacekeeping troops inside Ukraine along an as yet unnegotiated demarcation line . Unconfirmed leaks suggest the package includes as many as 40,000 troops , and a novel means to fund boosts to defence spending . The plan based on the model of postwar North and South Korea is so sensitive that no one yet wishes to discuss it in public . <p> The key drivers are Poland 's prime minister , Donald Tusk , in an alliance with the probable next German chancellor , Friedrich Merz , and the French president , Emmanuel Macron . The coalition needs to be credible enough both to convince Putin total victory is unachievable and to persuade Trump that Europe is reforming , and deserves American backing . <h> The Middle East and China <p> But just as Trump 's victory has forced the principals in Europe to rethink their war , Middle Eastern leaders wonder how their region 's proliferating and interconnected conflicts will be affected by Trump . Will he vacate the area , leaving the chaos to deepen , and allow other actors such as Turkey to regain their dominance and influence ? <p> Even Trump 's closest allies seem divided on how he will react . Some US diplomats brief : " Trump is not going to be like Bush or Obama . Sure , he 'll take calls from Gulf leaders , but he is going to respond : ' That 's your problem . ' " <p> Others such as Mike Waltz , the president-elect 's choice for national security adviser , say Trump is ready to make " big transformative deals " . Waltz is already claiming credit for the Lebanon ceasefire agreed before the inauguration . " Everyone 's coming to the table because of President Trump , " he claimed . <p> Yet Trump 's previous Middle East envoy Jason Greenblatt at the recent Doha forum for political dialogue said Trump saw no need to solve the Palestinian issue . " Many of you think the Palestinian issue is the be-all and end-all . Not true . What the Trump administration did , and I think they will try to do again , is to decouple the Palestinian issue from everything else . " He said that after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel " the Palestinian issue is so complicated and deeply entrenched , it is going to be hard to fix now " . <p> But that means the biggest deal -- the one between Saudi Arabia and Israel -- looks impossible for the moment . The Saudi crown prince , Mohammed bin Salman , has described what Israel has done in Gaza as a " genocide " , and his diplomats have said normalisation with Israel and an expansion of the Abraham accords -- bilateral agreements signed by Israel , the UAE and Bahrain during Trump 's first term -- is " off the table without a clear pathway to a Palestinian state " . <p> Moreover , just like Europe , the Gulf states are looking to reduce their reliance on the US . <p> Fawaz Gerges , a professor of the Middle East at the London School of Economics , pointed out : " Saudi Arabia , one of the most important Middle Eastern powers dependent on the US , is positioning itself for the Trump administration by diversifying its foreign policy , deepening its relations with China and normalising with Iran . " <p> He argued : " The Biden administration has insulted and humiliated its own Arab allies , all of which have been begging him to use leverage with the Israeli prime minister . " <p> The US , he contended , by " turning Israel into a military fortress , has prevented Israel from coming to terms with its neighbours . The US has not been a true friend of Israel since it has not sought to answer the question of : how do you anchor and integrate Israel into the social fabric in the region ? " <p> A self-confident Israel sees no need to answer such questions . The " military fortress " , after its display of dominance in 2024 , regards 2025 as the year to complete the remaking of the Middle East that it has begun in Gaza , Lebanon and Syria . <p> Within a week of the US election , the extremist Israeli cabinet member Bezalel Smotrich proclaimed that Trump 's return meant that " 2025 will , with God 's help , be the year of Israeli sovereignty in Judea and Samaria " -- the Israeli name for the West Bank . Annexation , an issue hotly contested within the first Trump administration , is back on the agenda , a prospect that terrifies the Gulf states . <p> More importantly , the stars may finally have aligned for Netanyahu to attack Iran 's nuclear sites , his objective for more than a decade . The authority says it wants to bring law and order to what 's long been a hotbed of militancy and a place where it has little control . <p> Its ability to contain armed groups there will reverberate far beyond the West Bank . The Palestinian Authority wants to position itself to take over governance in Gaza once the war there ends . But confronting Palestinians at a time when many view the authority as a subcontractor for Israel could deepen divisions in Palestinian society . <p> Here is a look at the days of fighting between Palestinians in the West Bank : <h> Fighting rages on the streets and at least 5 are dead <p> Earlier this month , security forces for the Western-backed Palestinian Authority stormed into Jenin refugee camp , a restive militant stronghold , and began a crackdown against armed groups . <p> Fighting has raged in the streets of the camp , and armored cars are seen patrolling . Palestinian security forces have taken over part of a hospital , using it as a base and shooting from inside , according to the United Nations . <p> At least one militant from the Islamic Jihad group and three security force members have been killed , including a captain in the intelligence services whose death was announced Wednesday , according to the Palestinian forces . About 50 people have been arrested . <p> At least two uninvolved civilians have been killed and some wounded . The fighting prompted the main U.N . agency for Palestinian refugees , UNRWA , to suspend its services , including schooling . The violence has disrupted safe access for Palestinians to other services , including water and health . It also has complicated the restoration of services destroyed in previous Israeli raids of the camp . <h> The Jenin refugee camp explained <p> The urban , built-up refugee camp in the northern West Bank houses Palestinians whose families were displaced in the 1948 war surrounding Israel 's creation . It has long been a center for Palestinian militancy and a bastion of armed struggle against Israel . The militant groups Islamic Jihad and Hamas operate freely there , and its streets are regularly lined with posters depicting slain fighters as martyrs for the Palestinian cause . <p> The Palestinian Authority , which administers the main Palestinian population centers of the West Bank as part of interim peace agreements with Israel from the 1990s , has little presence in Jenin . Many people view the Palestinian Authority forces with suspicion and see them as serving Israel 's interests because of security coordination that has facilitated Israel 's own crackdowns on Palestinians . <p> The refugee camp and the adjacent city of Jenin have long been targets of Israel in its stated bid to stamp out militancy . Since the start of the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza , which has sparked a wave of violence in the West Bank , Israel has raided or carried out airstrikes in Jenin multiple times , killing dozens and leaving heavy destruction . <p> Palestinian health officials say Israeli raids throughout the West Bank since Oct. 7 , 2023 , have killed more than 800 Palestinians . Israel says most of these are militants , but youth throwing stones and people not involved in confrontations have also been killed . <h> The PA raid is meant to restore order but it 's also linked to postwar Gaza <p> According to Brig . Gen. Anwar Rajab , the spokesperson for the Palestinian security forces , the raid is meant to impose law and order and restore peace and security . The troops were focused on " eradicating " Iran-backed groups that were trying to incite " chaos and anarchy , " he added . The raid will end when those goals are reached , according to the security forces . <p> But the raid is also shining a spotlight on the Palestinian Authority 's ability to impose order and security in a restive area . With no clear vision for who will administer postwar Gaza , the raid could convince skeptics that the authority has what it takes to rule the Palestinian enclave . Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is considering an agreement with Hamas that would create a committee of politically independent technocrats to administer the Gaza Strip after the war . The committee would report to him . <p> The Biden administration sees a rehabilitated Palestinian Authority as the best option to govern and secure postwar Gaza . The U.S. has for years invested heavily in training the Palestinian security forces , and the administration has seen its re-entry into Gaza , after being routed by Hamas in 2007 , as a feasible replacement for Hamas , whose rule Israel has sought to end with the war . <p> Israel rejects this idea , seeing the Palestinian Authority as too weak to be able to contain Hamas . It says it will maintain open-ended security control over Gaza . <p> The incoming Trump administration has not yet laid out its vision for postwar Gaza , but Trump 's first term was overwhelmingly supportive of Israel 's positions . <h> For Palestinians , the raid highlights and deepens their internal divisions <p> Palestinians are not strangers to divisions within their society , with the most prominent the rift between Hamas and Abbas ' Fatah party . The parties fought bloody street wars in Gaza before Hamas forced Fatah out of the territory , and the sides have failed to reconcile since . <p> Since then , the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority has tried to diminish Hamas ' influence in the West Bank , often with Israel 's help . <p> Reeling from the yearslong internal rift , Palestinians have staged general strikes and protests calling for unity . But the raid could deepen the perception of the Palestinian Authority as a facilitator of Israel 's whims and potentially undermine any popular support for it to return to effectively rule Gaza .

@@119282172 <p> " Forgive me Italy , " Hamada Shaqoura captioned one of his recent videos , in which he constructed a version of a pizza with a flatbread and a pan , before gifting the creation to a delighted child . <p> Gaza 's leading , and perhaps only remaining , food blogger has learned to make a virtue of necessity through 14 months of war , in which agriculture has been decimated and commercial imports cut off , leaving much of the population reliant on intermittent aid supplies . <p> For Shaqoura , 33 , that means a daily struggle to source the ingredients to maintain his hugely popular video series , in which he serves up improvised recipes from ' Gaza tacos ' -- with rare canned meat -- to cinnamon rolls , to the deprived residents of refugee camps . " <p> The quest for ingredients means scouring the sparse markets of southern Gaza , which offer unpredictable selections at inflated prices , as well as occasional prizes such as fresh produce and meat that Shaqoura has to be quick to secure . <p> The food blogger is among the 90 per cent of Gaza 's population that have been displaced at least once during the war . I am thinking of making many meals using chicken and meat , but unfortunately they are not available due to the siege . " <p> Food deprivation is having dire effects . " Every day under this aggression is a dangerous day . I try to maintain my safety and the safety of my family by staying away from some areas that are required to be evacuated , but there is no safety anywhere . " <p> Beyond shortages of ingredients , and the threat of Israeli bombs , the destruction of Gaza 's infrastructure also creates challenges for the blogger . He sometimes resorts to using wood fires when there is no gas or electricity to cook with . @@119283308 <p> In one of the most telling scenes from Kamal Aljafari 's Palestinian conceptual documentary , A Fidai Film , an Israeli soldier parades the theft of press clippings , books , and photos from across the Arab World that documented different facets of Palestinian life . <p> All of the material is taken to Israel in an all too familiar attempt to erase Palestine 's collective memory . <p> The depicted Israeli raid is rooted in an undeclared fear that these documents , which they regarded as propaganda , may harm Israel 's reputation or undermine the Zionist cause - a fear that acknowledges the power of the image and the word in challenging perceptions and convictions . <p> Forty years later , Israel is no longer concerned with Palestine 's pictorial memory . <p> The genocide of Gaza , the October 2024 war on Lebanon , and the recent raids on Syria have been played live in front of the world to no avail . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters <p> In 2024 , the image no longer holds any power or meaning . People have grown terribly distrustful of the image , of the word , of numbers , of the unadulterated truth . <p> In a post-truth world , everything can be manipulated , photoshopped , cropped , and fashioned into whatever narrative people wish to subscribe to . <p> But cinema still terrifies . <p> Cinema still unsettles , intimidates , and places that feared context to these images and words and numbers . <p> Cinema is dangerous , a thorn on the side of fundamentalists and fascists and the deliberately benighted . <p> And in 2024 , the intellectually emancipated Middle Eastern film has proven to be the most dangerous of them all . <p> Over the past 12 months , Middle Eastern films have been intensely scrutinised , debated , dismissed , celebrated , and in many cases , shunned by the mainstream establishment in both the West and the Middle East . <p> Not since the Arab Spring has Middle Eastern cinema felt so pertinent , so immediate , so insubordinate - be it in their inventive , challenging forms or truculent politics . <p> As Israel 's wars continued to rage on , the West remained clueless on how to deal with Middle Eastern cinema all throughout the year . <p> Alexis Bloom , the South African director of The Bibi Files pinpointed that the mainstream western film establishment is no longer interested in polarising and urgent political films , leaving exhibitions of Middle Eastern films in Europe and the US in the hands of few but valiant small distribution companies like the newly-formed Watermelon in the US and passionate film houses such as Wolf in Berlin . <p> The best of the year 's Middle Eastern cinema captured the zeitgeist of the global culture in a fashion that continues to elude a mainstream art primarily fixated on commerce and diversion . <p> In 2024 , the gap between the mainstream and the independent has grown so wide it 's now practically unbridgeable . <p> The increasing synergy between Egypt and Saudi Arabia continued to conflate , resulting most notably in Welaz Rizk 3 , the highest-grossing Egyptian film in history which doubled as a grand commercial for Riyadh . <p> Egypt produced a slew of middling entertainments that provided a distraction from the gruelling economic woes . Saudi , on the other hand , continued its industrial development , inaugurating the biggest film and TV studios in the Arabian Gulf while solidifying its position as the most lucrative film market in the region . <p> The rest of the region 's commercial cinema failed to strike a chord with viewers , hampered by the twin forces of self-censorship and the lack of funding from states that continues to treat cinema with caution and hostility . <p> Each of the following ten pictures faced colossal hurdles to see the light of day ; each has strived to attract a wide audience ; and collectively , they represent a brave act of defiance against totalitarianism , against the oppressive imperatives of the market , against the debilitating norms of an industry desperately striving for relevance . <p> So , without any further ado , here are the top most dangerous Middle Eastern films of 2024. <h> 10 ) Perfumed with Mint <p> The directorial debut of gifted Egyptian cinematographer Muhammad Hamdy is an atmospheric allegory about a group of men battling to contain the inexplicable sprouting of mint from their bodies with the use of hashish . <p> The aroma of the mint attracts foreboding shadows hunting down the defenceless folks who have lost all will to fight back . <p> Entirely conceived in a series of long , smouldering still frames that avidly nods to the work of Portuguese filmmaker Pedro Costa , Hamdy 's intrepid , rebellious work flouts the rules of classical storytelling long associated with Egyptian cinema , conjuring up a disorienting mist of a film about fear , trauma , and the overbearing stupefaction that has taken over the broken generation of the 2011 Revolution . <h> 9 ) Song of All Ends <p> The film follows the life of a family of six in the Shatila camp . We discover a family grieving the loss of their youngest daughter who died during the 2020 Beirut port explosion ( Giovanni C. Lorusso ) <p> Similarly evoking the films of Costa in his mythification of marginalised populations , the debut feature of Italian photographer turned filmmaker Giovanni C. Lorusso is an impressionistic , plotless monochrome portrait of a family residing in the rundown Lebanese refugee camp of Shatila . <p> The limited action of the film is largely comprised of the family 's quotidian existence whose stillness cloaks simmering grief derived from the loss of their youngest daughter in the 2020 Beirut explosion . <p> Shot in 2023 , the recent evacuation of the camp in the wake of Israeli strikes on Southern Lebanon last October imbues the picture with an additional tint of pathos . <h> 8 ) East of Noon <p> " Once upon a time , there were frightened people . They were so frightened that their imagination escaped . " <p> Thus begins the sophomore effort of visual artist and filmmaker Hala Elkoussy , a musical fable about a young musician aspiring to break free from his poverty-stricken , autocratically-ruled fictional small town . <p> Shot in black and white and laced with disparate influences -- from the colloquial Arabic poetry of Salah Jahin and Egyptian musicals of the 1940s , to the use of political symbolism in the Brazilian Cinema Novo , East of Noon is the year 's most formally inventive picture : an anti-realistic political parable examining one the most pressing questions facing Middle Eastern art today : is art a means of rebellion or a mere tool in the arsenal of autocracy to sedate the masses ? <p> Like Perfumed with Mint , Elkoussy employs fantasy to work around censorship , illustrating in the process that political cinema can still manage to be produced in the most tyrannical of systems . <h> 7 ) From Ground Zero <p> Each film in From Ground Zero , ranging from 3 to 7 minutes , presents a unique perspective on the current reality in Gaza ( Masharawi Films Fund ) <p> In the aftermath of 7 October , veteran Palestinian filmmaker Rashid Masharawi lent cameras to a group of 22 amateur Palestinian directors to document and reflect on their daily hardships in Gaza amidst the mounting Israeli aggression . <p> The result is a miracle of a film : a highly singular anthology of short films seeping with pain , despair , hope , and ultimately resilience shot by aspiring artists whose fate remains in peril . <p> Traversing diverse genres - from animation and fantasy to social realism and verit ? -- and varying in tone and sentiment , From Ground Zero is a rare portal into the lives of ordinary Palestinians as they toil to fathom and adapt to the inescapable death and destruction surrounding them . <p> The Palestinians of From Ground Zero are the numbers the world has kept a blind eye on ; the innocent lives entrapped in an inferno they ca n't get out of . <p> The splatter of optimism , of perseverance , fashioned by the Gazan women filmmakers as a form of dignified resistance makes for some of the most powerful moments in any film this year , challenging what cinema is and what it could be . <h> 6 ) A Fidai Film <p> Veteran experimental Palestinian filmmaker Kamal Aljafari has conjured up a fascinating oeuvre out of reclaiming the Palestinian collective memory by reappropriating historical footage and resurrecting the Palestinian pictorial presence that has been wiped out by the Israeli colonisers . <p> Culled from rare footage stolen by the IDF during the Lebanese Civil War in 1982 , A Fidai Film is similar in intention and method to his 2015 feature , Recollection , but is more expansive in scope and angrier in pitch : a railing cry against a history that been stolen and distorted , a history that routinely went by unchallenged since 1948 . <p> Punctuated by the lyrical ruminations of the late great writer Ghassan Kanafani , A Fidai Film is a dense if playful and stirring film that questions our naive belief in the veracity of the image while exposing the hazardous role of narration : a simultaneous act of disruption and self-affirmation against time , against violent depletion , against fate . <h> 5 ) Who Do I Belong To <p> Aicha lives in the isolated north of Tunisia with her husband and youngest son . Oscar-nominated short , Brotherhood , with the striking debut : a supernatural mystery about an ex-Isis fighter returning to his northern Tunisian home , with an enigmatic burqa-wearing wife , before a series of murders shakes up the harmony of his village . <p> A genre-subverting serial killer pic conceived as a naturalistic reverie similar in look and feel to the mediative work of American @@119287113 <p> Whatever label you apply -- the woke , the hard Left , progressives -- it 's been a lousy year for acolytes of the " omnicause " . We are finally seeing a retreat on the big issues that animate the kinds of activists who chuck soup over old paintings , harangue feminists or turn some parts of London into no-go areas for Jews every Saturday . <p> It 's not that the activists have gone away or the chanting has stopped , but that the nastiness and arrogance of these campaigns are alienating more and more people and in the process becoming less and less effective . Their delusions are wearing as thin as a culturally-appropriated keffiyeh and they only have themselves to blame : 2024 has been the year of the backlash . <p> This boneheadedness of the hard Left was there on election day in July outside my local polling station . I was greeted for the umpteenth time that month by supporters of Faiza Shaheen , who was standing as an independent candidate in Woodford Green and Chingford ( ostensibly on Gaza ) after being deselected by Labour a few weeks before . I asked one of her fanboys why Shaheen had not rejected the endorsement of dictator-adjacent George Galloway . His response was to start screaming that I was not entitled to an opinion . I suggested that by standing against Labour , Shaheen and her petulant followers would most likely split the Left and allow the Conservatives to keep the seat . " She will win ! " he spat in my general direction . I hate to say I told you so but ... actually I love to say I told you so . It was all there in that moment : he was aggressive , one-eyed and wrong . <p> The big problem for social justice warriors now is that on every issue about which they have chosen to obsess ( to the detriment of any constructive , meaningful ideas ) the result is pushback . It 's almost as if people do n't like being patronised and insulted . <p> Whatever " woke " is ( it 's such an incoherent ecosystem that finding a satisfactory name is virtually impossible ) it 's not the same as minority rights or protection of the vulnerable . Woke extremism is nihilistic , offering up performative moralism instead of answers . Progressives adopt the catchphrase of Roald Dahl 's Harry Wormwood , Matilda 's useless father : " I 'm smart , you 're dumb ; I 'm big , you 're little ; I 'm right , you 're wrong . " <p> On the environment , extremists ' stated reason for their direct action is that it has to be disruptive to draw attention to the urgency of the crisis . It has to be dramatic to force people out of their slumber . Yet the tactics employed by the likes of Just Stop Oil have the opposite effect . Throwing soup over venerated works of art has made the protestors look like the posh pranksters they are and little else . Disrupting roads and train stations does n't just annoy people , but does real harm to their lives . What has it all achieved ? Even less engagement with the issues , a nationwide shake of the head at the vanity of it all and prison sentences for the perpetrators . <p> Greta Thunberg embodies the slow decline of the progressives ' power to influence in 2024 . Where once she could wag her finger at world leaders and they would quiver in fear , she 's become irrelevant , appearing to have abandoned her once beloved Planet Earth for the cause of Palestinians and the grandstanding " River To The Sea " crowd . As a child she articulated the rage of a generation . As a young woman , she looks like just another student with an Israel obsession . <p> More broadly , pro-Palestinian activists are now facing the realities of global politics . As the year ends , the situation in the Middle East shows the limits of a movement that offers no solutions . So these once noisy advocates should be looking for compromises to resolve undeniable sticking points , thereby helping trans people live better , safer lives . They do n't seem to have considered that bringing people in is more effective than forcing them out . And if they thought 2024 was rough , Donald Trump is sure to have some more bad news for them in 2025.

@@119292540 <h> The photographs that defined 2024 -- and the stories behind them <p> Policing at a football match in Spain . Photograph : Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters <p> As conflict dragged on in Gaza and Ukraine , violence dogged the US election ; floods and fires raged , but bravery and humanity shone through . Photographers recall the moments when they took these era-defining photos <h> London , UK , 24 April <p> Two horses bolt through central London Jordan Pettitt <p> I was on Aldwych in London , outside the building where the inquiry into the Post Office scandal was being heard , and I 'd finished photographing people going in . A few of us were standing around , flicking through pictures and chatting , then all of a sudden , the normally busy street fell silent . Cars and buses had vanished . <p> You could hear it first -- the thundering of hooves -- and these two horses appeared at the top of the road . People must have stopped and slowed down to let these horses bolt straight through . I ran to the pavement edge , whipped up the camera and managed to get a few frames as they sped past . I initially thought that the red colour on one of the horses was paint . Only when it got nearer did I realise it was blood . <p> The only thing that was going through my mind was the colour of that horse , and just thinking that was a red I had n't seen before , it was so rich . It was all so quick that you do n't get time to think about anything else other than make sure the camera is pointing in the right direction . It was all over in seconds , completely random , and we just managed to be in the right spot at the right time . <p> It made the news very quickly -- the horses had been on a training exercise at the barracks near Buckingham Palace , got spooked , thrown off their riders and bolted . Fortunately , they were safely caught . <h> Mexico-US border , 26 March <p> A man carrying his daughter waits before attempting to cross into the US Brandon Bell <p> It was sunset , and temperatures were dropping pretty fast . Every maybe 30 minutes , somebody within a group would use pliers or cutters to try to cut through the barbed wire . <p> Earlier that week , there was a major clash on the border and border patrol had doubled down , so security around the area was really tight . Jordan was one of around 30 people in a group , which included children . He was carrying his daughter , wrapped in a blanket , while her mother was trying to sort out a plan with the rest of the group . They have a quick window -- maybe 45 seconds , not even a minute -- once they get to the razor wire , to make it through before law enforcement swarm that area and close it down . <p> He had stepped away from the group and just stood in this valley , looking at the fence and looking at the other side . When I saw him , I thought that it showed struggle , but also determination to make it across by any means necessary . He 's trying to keep his daughter warm , and he 's just waiting patiently for the group to come up with a plan . <p> He did make it across with his family , but others who followed got right to the wire and were turned around . When they make it through , they run , before border officials can get them into SUVs and take them to be processed . <h> Valencia , Spain , 1 November <p> Cars and debris pile up by a bridge after the flooding in Valencia David Ramos <p> I had headed straight to Valencia after the floods , and was one of the first outsiders to arrive at the villages near the city . People would shout out of their windows asking if someone was coming to help , and where had I come from . It was quite shocking how little information they had -- no television , no phones , the communications were down . I walked for miles . It was like a tsunami , the destruction . That feeling of shock turned into anger at the management of everything , from the alerts the day before the floods , and then the devastation everywhere . At least 200 people lost their lives . <p> This photograph was taken three days after the flood . I was walking towards the village of Benet ? sser , outside Valencia , along the railway track -- it was the easiest way to reach it . A lot of people from the village used the track to get water , or food , from Valencia . I saw some firefighters pumping water at an underpass under a railway bridge , and when I went to the other side , I found that wall of cars . I was amazed at the power of the water . <p> The emergency services were there , analysing the situation . I think they were looking for bodies in the cars , but luckily none were found . Then they were working out how to move the cars , one by one . I was there for a couple of hours , but I know it took a couple of days to clear the underpass . <h> Florida , US , 26 September <p> The US coast guard rescues a man and his dog during Hurricane Helene <p> Twenty-five miles off Florida 's Sanibel Island , a sailing boat began taking on water and called for help . Josh Edgoose <p> I 've been wanting to go to the Portsmouth kite festival for a long time . I thought it might have been a plane that came down . I did n't have my cameras with me , but I had my phone , so I took a motorbike taxi and headed in the direction of the fire , even though the roads were blocked . <p> It turned out to be a depot where they keep secondhand drums of oil paint , so when they started burning , the flames went up so fast . I had to pocket my phone tightly and find a way out -- someone on a motorbike was trying to leave and I asked him to drop me back in the city centre . The fire kept burning until morning . <h> Donbas region , Ukraine , 18 April <p> The tattooed hands of a commander Tom Peter <p> Roman is 38 and a commander of a sniper support unit . He left Ukraine years ago and settled in France . He said he had everything he ever dreamed of , but then the war started , and he signed up because he felt he could n't look at himself in the mirror if he was sitting this out . So he went back to his home country to fight . We were in Donbas region and spent four or five days with him and his men in various dugouts . He has a reconnaissance drone unit , a mortar unit , and active fighting personnel , and they fan out across a section of the frontline . @@119292894 <p> Whether you 're commuting through festive chaos or embarking on a long journey to visit family , a great podcast can transform your travel experience this Christmas . From thrilling true crime stories to brain-enhancing tips , our critics have curated a list of the best pods to keep you entertained and engaged . Featuring everyone from Peter Mandelson to Richard Osman , Louis Theroux to Lauren Laverne , this is your ultimate guide . <h> True crime <h> Kill List <p> The big true crime hit of 2024 . Four years ago the British investigative tech journalist Carl Miller discovered a murder-for-hire website on the dark web . Intimate , hate-filled messages had been posted detailing targets ' names , addresses and daily routines . Payments were made in bitcoin . Even if the site were not what it seemed , did Miller have a moral obligation to alert potential victims ? This may initially present as just another true crime podcast , but it has an original , twisting , involving tale to tell . And not only a retrospective one . Patricia Nicol <h> Shadow World : Thief at the British Museum <p> Perhaps the best thing the BBC made in 2024 was this quietly gripping investigation into the theft of antique jewels from the British Museum , hosted by the corporation 's culture editor , Katie Razzall . It 's like something from the golden age of crime fiction and has a marvellous central character in the Danish antiquities dealer Dr Ittai Gradel , whose " photographic memory " helped him to spot the museum 's treasures being sold online . James Marriott <h> To Catch a Scorpion <p> " I was scaring . So much cold , " Marianne , seven , says , recalling the journey to the UK that almost killed her family , when their small boat shattered . At the top of the human chain exploiting desperate migrants , kingpin smugglers are making a killing . The BBC investigative reporter Sue Mitchell and the aid worker Rob Lawrie set out to track down Barzan Majeed , aka the Scorpion , an Iraqi Kurd with a pitiless reputation , sought by prosecutors internationally . Joining this brave pair on his trail makes for gripping , informative , worthwhile listening . PN <h> Cocaine Inc <p> What do the murder of Elle Edwards on Christmas Eve , 2022 , drug tunnels under the US-Mexican border and shoot-outs in suburban Sydney have in common ? Cocaine , the ubiquitous , illegal substance fuelling crime globally . For this hit investigative series spanning four continents and 30,000 miles , reporters from The Times , The Sunday Times and News Corp Australia have teamed up to expose the economics , powder trail and unglamorous truths about a habit so common " it 's likely that you , or someone you know , has snorted a line recently " . PN <h> Advertisement <h> Culture <p> Richard Osman and Marina Hyde present The Rest Is Entertainment <h> The Rest Is Entertainment <p> Marina Hyde , the journalist , and the TV personality turned author Richard Osman talk over the triumphs and the tragedies of the entertainment industry . Both are brimming over with insider knowledge . What makes a good quiz format ? How does a reality TV show get made ? Will AI really destroy Hollywood ? Is the age of the superhero franchise film finally over ? It 's also a great source of recommendations if you 're not sure what to watch , read or listen to . PN <h> The Wonder of Stevie <p> This show is a blaze of sunshine . Its primary focus is the breathtaking achievement of Stevie Wonder 's genre-defying five-album stint from Music of My Mind in 1972 to Songs in the Key of Life in 1976 . In passing , the ebullient presenter Wesley Morris , an unstuffy Pulitzer prizewinner , surveys Motown , civil rights and black American culture . The series is made by Barack and Michelle Obama 's media company , Higher Ground , and concludes with the former president chatting to Wonder . A joy . PN <h> London Review of Books Podcast <p> The London Review of Books podcast is just as intelligent and eclectic as the magazine . The hosts are Malin Hay , Adam Shatz and Thomas Jones and their guests tackle everything ... and we mean everything . Recent episodes deal with the novels of JG Ballard , the architecture of the 16th century , the bombing of Gaza , acid house rave , the difficulties of translating Proust into English , the infected blood scandal , cryptocurrency fraud and Chaucer 's debt to Ovid . Did they miss anything ? PN <h> Advertisement <h> Broaden your mind <h> Uncharted with Hannah Fry <p> The newly minted Cambridge professor of the public understanding of mathematics more than does justice to her title with her superb BBC Radio 4 show about statistics . Through a series of deftly told stories , she shows how mastery of numbers can save our lives . The best episode concerns how the US coast guard used ingenious computer modelling to work out the location of people lost at sea . JM <h> The Rest Is Classified <p> The latest offering from Gary Lineker 's podcasting juggernaut , Goalhanger Studios , delves into the murky history of espionage . The hosts , the former CIA analyst David McCloskey and the journalist Gordon Corera , offer glimpses of " what really goes on in the secret world " . The Rest Is Classified follows the unbeatable Goalhanger formula of great stories , dubious jokes and a sprinkle of behind-the-scenes insight . JM <h> Misquoting Jesus <p> This podcast was n't launched this year but it was new to us , and it 's so good that it deserves a mention . The Biblical scholar Bart Ehrman offers weekly deep dives into the early history of Christianity : did Jesus exist ? Who wrote the gospels ? Why did the Christian faith spread so fast ? It sounds esoteric , but Ehrman is the kind of charismatic expert who could bring any subject alive . Fans of The Rest Is History will love it . JM <h> The History Podcast : The Brighton Bomb <p> Amid a stellar year for series about the IRA , this stands out for the Northern Irish writer Glenn Patterson 's meticulous storytelling . Known historical events unfold like a thriller , reverberating with what-ifs . The background thrum of unease that was such a feature of that era of UK bombing campaigns is evoked vividly . Should you seek more , other BBC recommendations include The History Podcast : Escape from the Maze , In Detail ... The Pub Bombings and the still-to-conclude Cover : Stakeknife . PN <h> The Studies Show <p> The science journalists Tom Chivers and Stuart Ritchie dig down into the lurid science headlines ( the " can satsumas give you Alzheimer 's ? " genre of journalism ) to pick apart the studies behind them . The result is rigorous ( prepare to hear lots about sample sizes and " p hacking " ) but fascinating . What actually is addiction ? Is loneliness really as bad for you as smoking ? Does depression exist ? A reminder that the best entertainment comes from treating your audience as if ( shock horror ) they are intelligent people . PN <h> Advertisement <h> Past Present Future <p> David Runciman , the Cambridge politics professor turned podcaster , provides an erudite spin through the history of political thought . Recent highlights include episodes on the great political fictions ( featuring George Eliot 's Middlemarch , Salman Rushdie 's Midnight 's Children and Margaret Atwood 's The Handmaid 's Tale ) . Especially good is the history of bad ideas : episodes on antisemitism , mesmerism and the case against giving women the vote . PN <h> Documentary <h> Three Million <p> Even in India not enough is known about the estimated three million people who died of starvation between 1943 and 1944 . In Britain , when people have heard of the Bengal famine , it is often regarded as a slur on the reputation of Winston Churchill . Kavita Puri 's rigorous , illuminating , emotionally resonant BBC series set out to address that . Deservedly , since its release in February , this award-winning series has had real impact internationally . In a follow-up episode listeners meet the final generation of survivors . A book will follow . PN <h> Things Fell Apart <p> The second series of Jon Ronson 's wonderful BBC podcast about the history of the culture wars launched at the beginning of the year . Ronson tackles such thorny issues as changing definitions of " trauma " , the grievances of men 's rights activists and fights over gender . Almost nobody manages to approach these issues really impartially , but Ronson is a model of even-handed common sense . JM <h> The Secret Life of Prisons <p> This podcast has been one of the year 's revelations . I first listened to it to better understand the prisons crisis . It is impressively wide-ranging : episodes have included an ex-convict 's account of how an HMP Feltham PE instructor helped him to shed 18 stone ; Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe 's Longford lecture , " What I learnt about prison in Iran " ; poignant insights into parenting from behind bars ; and a criminal justice-focused budget analysis . Phil Maguire , of the Prison Radio Association , presents with the excellently intuitive broadcaster Paula Harriott , who told her story in an October episode , From Cell to CEO . PN <h> The Gift <p> Jenny Kleeman 's two-series BBC show tracks the stories of people who were given DNA home test kits as gifts . From these innocuous beginnings , a Pandora 's box of information spills out : unwelcome discoveries relating to paternity , shocking tales of medical malpractice and poignant accounts of suddenly discovered siblings and ancestries . These stories are strong ( the episode Sold deserves to win awards ) , and Kleeman unobtrusively lets them tell themselves , with minimal prompting and imposed narration . PN <h> Advertisement <h> Hysterical <p> Outbreaks of mass hysteria ( or , as we 're advised to call them nowadays , mass psychogenic illness ) are always a good source of podcasting material . In Hysterical , Dan Taberski tackles an outbreak of twitching , stuttering and tics at a New York high school . Sensible listeners know all along that it 's nothing to do with crop dusters , fracking or chemical spills , but these theories help to spin things out enjoyably enough , and the story is so strange that it repays the listener 's attention anyway . JM <h> Comedy <h> What Did You Do Yesterday ? <p> Feel dogged by your to-do lists ? Is time not so much a winged chariot as a condemned Lada ? Then this comedy podcast revelling in quotidian failings ( although not criticising get-up-and-go ) is for you . The hosts , the comedian David O'Doherty and the radio presenter Max Rushden , ask their title question then consider the life-in-the-day-of answers of guests such as James Acaster , Rose Matafeo , Alex Horne and Richard Osman . A stupidly simple idea , beautifully executed . PN <h> Everything Is News <p> This is a glorious send up of self-important news podcasts . The comedians Michael Clarke and Helen Price play the " troubled former Tory cabinet minister Tom Dudley-Brown " and the pompous BBC grande dame Julia Markham . Together they witter on pointlessly about all the glamorous international conferences they 've attended , offer hilariously out-of-touch commentary on how ordinary people live and prosecute grudges against professional rivals . JM <h> News and politics <h> How to Win an Election <p> The Times 's hit politics podcast relaunched this year with Hugo Rifkind at the helm . He is joined by Daniel Finkelstein , Peter Mandelson and Polly MacKenzie to pick over the latest from Westminster . We 're obviously biased , but in a world of po-faced and depressing politics commentary this one stands out for its wit and sparkle . JM <h> Hacks on Tap <p> As the terrifying spectacle of a second Donald Trump presidency looms ever closer , Hacks on Tap remains the essential guide to politics across the Pond . Our hosts are two affable old hands : the Obama campaign adviser David Axelrod and the Republican ( but Trump-loathing ) political strategist Mike Murphy . It 's supposed to feel like you 've sat down at a bar to chat politics with two of the best informed men in the business . It works beautifully . PN <h> Advertisement <h> These Times <p> Tom McTague , a journalist , and the mega-brain academic Helen Thompson chat through the deep trends underlying the news . This is pretty much the opposite of the sort of politics show that sticks to trivial Westminster gossip . While lesser podcasters are prattling about what Priti Patel said about James Cleverly in the House of Commons lunch queue , McTague and Thompson are digging into global oil markets , Europe 's structural geopolitical disadvantages and the future of autocracy . It requires concentration , but it 's deeply refreshing . PN <h> Frank Off the Radio <p> In March Frank Skinner announced on air that he had been sacked by Absolute Radio , where for 15 years he had headlined a much-loved Saturday morning show . Now he and his redundant radio sidekicks , Emily Dean and Pierre Novellie , are back with a podcast offering their clever , chucklesome , convolutedly looping chat , only without musical interruption . Funny friends reunited . His poetry podcast is here too . PN <h> The Sports Agents <p> Gabby Logan and Mark Chapman host this new podcast which rather dauntingly covers all sport : cycling , the Olympics , rugby , mixed martial arts , Formula 1 , horse racing , football , American football ... You name it , they 've got it covered . This inevitably makes for a slightly diffuse show . It is kept alive by Logan and Chapman 's amazing breadth of knowledge and their buoyant and professional presenting styles . Other shows will go deeper , but if you want to keep on top of what is happening in literally all sport , this is the place to be . PN <h> Interview <h> Strangers on a Bench <p> The singer-songwriter Tom Rosenthal wanders around London parks and talks to strangers sitting on benches . A simple idea but a wonderful one . The ensuing conversations are funny and moving . Rosenthal 's unmissable episode is The Disappearing Cyclist , a chat with a man who decided to abandon his life and cycle to India after a chance conversation with two strangers in a Bethnal Green pub . It could be a novel . JM <h> The Louis Theroux Podcast <p> This show used to be on the BBC as Grounded with Louis Theroux . Like pretty much all BBC stars , Theroux has been poached by a wealthy private company -- in this instance Spotify . I liked this podcast better when it was still on the Beeb , but even so it 's hard to go far wrong with Theroux 's faux-diffident interviewing style , which is an unbeatable tool for winkling information out of reluctant celebs . Recent guests include Baz Luhrmann , Germaine Greer and Sharon Stone . PN <h> Surprise yourself ... <h> Hyperfixed <p> Alex Goldman is a former host of Reply All , the show famous for producing what is sometimes called the greatest podcast episode ever , The Case of the Missing Hit . His long-awaited new show is just as good . Tenaciously following listener queries ( why do n't supermarket fridges have doors ? Is it possible to convert American cups to grams accurately ? ) , he ends up in fascinating , bizarre and philosophical places . It 's really wonderful . JM <h> The Mysterious Affair at Styles <p> If a classic crime adaptation is on your Christmas list , then this is one for which it 's worth breaking out the brandy ( and smelling salts ? ) . Set during the First World War , as in Agatha Christie 's debut novel , this introduces Hercule Poirot ( Peter Dinklage ) as he boards a refugee ship from Belgium . Superb sound design and a cracking cast , including Himesh Patel as Captain Hastings , Harriet Walter and Patsy Ferran , make this indulgently pleasurable audio for a darkening winter 's day . PN <h> Shows worth returning to <h> The Rest Is History <p> Possibly the most joyous and brain-enhancing podcast out there . Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are deeply well-informed historians , but also a brilliant comic double act . Together they delve into history , ancient and modern . There is a refreshingly irreverent old-school flavour to proceedings . No pious moaning about the sins of the past , but lots of jokes about the French . Recent highlights include a series on the life of Martin Luther , the sinking of the Titanic and the history of the suit . PN <h> The Story <p> The flagship news podcast from The Times , with Manveen Rana as lead presenter , tells just one story in depth . Sometimes that story is what you would expect from the day 's news agenda . But many of the most thought-provoking episodes take listeners behind the headlines to recount something more intimate and illuminating ; for example , the crime correspondent David Woode recounting his experiences of police stop and search as a young black man . Another remarkable episode was the Times Gaza correspondent Amal Helles 's A Diary of War : Three Months in Gaza . The data journalist Matilda Davies 's Every Scary Thing Meta Knows About You was chastening . PN <h> Just One Thing <p> This series of programmes from Michael Mosley , who died on holiday this year , provides small tips for living a healthier , happier life . All are gratifyingly easy to implement : improve your brain power by putting your phone down , go swimming because it could be the most effective form of exercise , swap sugar for fruit , take a cold shower , go for a daily walk . Wonderful stuff . PN <h> The Rest Is Politics <p> If you have n't heard of this you must have been hiding under a rock with your fingers in your ears . Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart host the UK 's most popular politics podcast . Both men draw on their careers in government to pick apart events in Westminster and beyond . They really hate Brexit and Boris Johnson . The Rest Is Politics is increasingly good on foreign affairs . If you want a lucid overview of what 's going down in the Bundestag right now , Campbell has you covered . PN <h> Where Should We Begin ? with Esther Perel <p> Would n't you love the chance to eavesdrop on other people 's therapy sessions ? On Where Should We Begin ? , the wonderfully accented Belgian psychotherapist Esther Perel talks couples through their relationship issues . Part of the pleasure comes from how eye-poppingly complicated other people 's lives are ( what on earth do you do when you find out your husband has secretly donated his sperm to his lesbian best friend ? ) . But also Perel is genuinely wise about people and feelings . PN <h> Off Menu <p> Podcast restaurant royalty James Acaster and Ed Gamble are now 12 seasons into running their " dream restaurant " , in which funny guests pick their fantasy meal . Brooklyn Nine-Nine 's Jason Mantzoukas talking ruefully about his egg allergy ( he once had to break off kissing a first date to rush to hospital because she 'd had a foam on a cocktail ) rounded off season 11 nicely . PN <h> Desert Island Discs <p> This is still the best interview format yet invented . Guests tell the story of their lives through their eight favourite records . Lauren Laverne has had some fascinating recent guests : the comedian Greg Davies , the actress Rebel Wilson and the novelist John Boyne . The archive is the real joy . Desert Island Discs has hosted pretty much every famous name you can think of in any field you care to name . The early episodes with Roy Plumley are a passport to another age . PN <h> Off Air with Jane and Fi <h> Backlisted <p> John Mitchinson and Andy Miller 's much-loved long-running literary show invites guests to discuss a favourite old book . Recent episodes include the thriller writer Alex Michaelides on Ford Madox Ford 's The Good Soldier , Andrew Hunter Murray on PD James 's The Children of Men and the poet Emily Berry on Anne Sexton 's All My Pretty Ones . PN <h> In Our Time <p> Melvyn Bragg may be 85 and this BBC treasure-trove past its 1,000th episode , but this flagship , one of the BBC 's most downloaded podcasts globally with a strong under-35s following , remains in splendid fettle . Every episode , since 1998 , is available to download . If you are at a loss where to start , the In Our Time archive offers curated guides under headings such as Listeners ' Top 10 , Religion , Philosophy , Science , History and more . @@119293573 <h> The film is n't an apology for colonialism <h> Share <h> What critics get wrong about Zulu <p> It is a great mystery how Zulu , a tale of imperial derring-do from the Anglo-Zulu war of 1879 , has avoided being cancelled . On the face of it , this is a film that revels in one of the most heinous , most blood-thirsty chapters of our colonial past , one tinged with technologically enabled white supremacy . Here is a war film about 140 white Europeans who take on a Zulu force of 4,000 and defeat them , thanks largely to the rapid and orchestrated fire of short-chamber Martini-Henry rifles . ( ' And a bayonet , ' as Nigel Green , as colour sergeant Bourne , puts it , ' with some guts behind it . ' ) <p> In the age of Zulu , colonialism was n't just a discredited idea , it was finished <p> So it was especially gratifying to see it once again on Channel Four over the Christmas break , albeit with a trigger warning of ' nudity , battlefield violence and language and attitudes of the era that may offend ' ? ? ? -- all rather like flagging up ' iceberg-related trauma ' ahead of a showing of Titanic . <p> And yet watch Zulu and you discover that it is anything but a celebration of colonialism or blood-soaked jingoism -- or indeed of racial supremacy of any particular kind . In fact , a smash hit on its release in 1964 , 60 years ago this month , the film continues to be highly regarded -- the BFI ranked it 31st in its 1999 list of the greatest British films of the 20th century , while Empire magazine has it in 33rd place in its 2023 list of the greatest 100 British films of all time ( sandwiched between A Man For All Seasons and 1995 's Sense and Sensibility ) . <p> In part the secret of Zulu 's enduring appeal lies in the personalities at its heart : first , for a film supposedly about a British imperial success , it was directed and co-produced by Cy Endfield , an American filmmaker who was only in Britain in the 1960s because he had been black-listed in Hollywood for his youthful involvement in communist activism . In him , then , there was no friend of British imperialism . Which explains the next part of the formula : the casting of working class-lad , Michael Caine , in his first major role , playing against type as an upper-class officer . Caine has said that no English director would have cast him in the role ; it took a classless American and communist sympathiser to get his career off the ground . We also have the film 's then star and co-producer , Stanley Baker , a Labour-party supporter born into a coal-mining family in South Wales . Between them the still-fresh screenplay by John Prebble -- a Brit who also happened to be a communist andhad a Native American great aunt no less ? ? -- there is a decidedly sardonic gloss to this tale of British imperial military steadfastness . As well as veering between evocative scene setting and ever mounting jeopardy ( along with Shakespearian-lite comic turns from the rank and file ) , the script crucially laces the eventual ' victory ' of the British with a convincing bitterness . It also makes a string of jabs at Britain 's social hierarchy , rather more prevalent and potent in the 1960s then than now . ( Indeed , do n't forget that Alec Douglas-Home , the 14th Earl of Home , was in No. 10 when the film came out . ) <h> Most popular <h> Gangster released early by Labour mocks Sir Keir in Christmas song <p> Some critics have claimed that the film is disingenuous , that it serves up pacificist pieties in order to paper over its glorification of the military action . It 's hard not to have some sympathy for the position , but I would argue that a balance is achieved . Moreover the film is not blood-thirsty by modern standards . While the body-count is high , if you compare the depictions of violence in it to a film like The Revenant , say , then Zulu looks about as tame as an episode of Hey Duggee . <p> Among those who clearly agreed that the filmmakers got it right was one of its other stars , the South African politician , tireless anti-Apartheid campaigner and Zulu prince Chief Buthelezi , who died last year aged 95 , having served for a decade in the governments of South African presidents Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki . As well as portraying his great-grandfather , King Cetshwayo ( whom he apparently resembled ) , Buthelezi remained a fan of the film ? -- which doubtlessly bolstered a sense of Zulu patriotism ? -- and attended a 50th anniversary screening of the film alongside Prince Harry and Stanley Baker 's widow in London in 2014 . In 2018 , amid criticism of the film , Buthelezi defended it , telling the Times : ' Even if the past is uncomfortable , and perhaps especially when the past is uncomfortable , it needs to be examined and unpacked rather than hidden away . Of course race is a central theme in the film . ' <p> Which is the point , is n't it ? Because for all that Zulu makes for an exciting **25;332;TOOLONG film , it also wears its heart and politics on its sleeve . Here is a film that is a product of its time -- the early 1960s , when colonialism was about as in vogue as it is now . Between Macmillan 's winds of change speech in February 1960 and the release of the film in January 1964 , no fewer than six African colonies gained independence from Britain , including Nigeria , Kenya and Uganda . By 1968 , another seven had gone . In the age of Zulu , colonialism was n't just a discredited idea , it was finished . <p> The film is far from perfect , of course . While the arc of the story is accurate , it takes liberties with the truth . In reality , for instance , Henry Hook , the disorderly private played by James Booth in the film , was a teetotaller and model soldier whose daughters walked out of the premier of the film in disgust at his portrayal . Naturally , there will be those who believe that it does n't go far enough to distance itself from the horrors its depicting . <p> What we can say for certain is that Zulu endures in part because it 's undoubtedly a thrilling tale , but primarily because it 's a war film is about survival not victory . It 's a film that celebrates human courage , not imperialism . And while it contains racists ? -- characters who betray the social mores of the Victorian era ? -- it is itself unracist , since , as anyone who 's seen it knows , the British only get through the ordeal by adopting the preferred military tactics of the Zulus themselves and therefore learning from them . That we are not spared the appalling human consequences of mechanical firepower as Cy Endfield 's camera slowly pans across the slain Zulu bodies very deliberately tells you all you need to know . Whatever their pre-existing prejudices those that live depart with an elevated respect for their foes . ( As one of the Welshmen puts it : ' I think they 've got more guts than we have , boyo ' . ) <p> So do n't shy away from Zulu and , if you have n't watched it in a while take another glance . The Drakensberg Mountains are stunning , the skies razor sharp ; there 's Nigel Green 's wonderfully understated colour sergeant Bourne and then there 's that astonishingly bombastic John Barry score which could have adorned a John Ford Western . All these , plus the departing salute of the vast Zulu impi , will leave you in no doubt that this remains a highly complex and culturally important film , and one that was certainly ahead of its time . <h> This article is free to read <p> To unlock more articles , subscribe to get 3 months of unlimited access for just $5 <h> Share <h> What critics get wrong about Zulu <h> Read next <p> On a steamy August morning in 2019 , I went to Sunday mass in Gaza city 's Church of the Holy Family .
