@@119362774 <h> Will Israel bomb Iran -- and 3 more questions for the world in 2025 <h> Whether it 's China , Ukraine , Trump or the Middle East , Britain will have to tread carefully , a former foreign policy adviser in No 10 writes <p> John Bew <p> Saturday December 28 2024 , 3.55pm , The Sunday Times <p> It is likely to be a pivotal year in the making or breaking of the modern world , with profound consequences for the United Kingdom . <p> Indeed , it is hard to think of a period in postwar history in which foreign policy has the potential to alter the lives of people in this country so dramatically , from their bank bills to their personal security . <h> Hard choices <p> Kyivites take shelter in a subway station during an air raid alert on Christmas Day <p> THOMAS PETER/REUTERS <p> Since Russia 's invasion of Ukraine , we have seen the growing alignment of our adversaries around the world -- Iran , Russia , China and North Korea -- and their increased willingness to support each other with diplomatic cover , sanctions evasion , lethal weaponry , technological subsistence for their defence industrial bases and now , in the case of North Korea 's intervention against Ukraine , the sending of troops to fight and die in each other 's wars . <p> In response , a quantum leap is required in the way we reimagine , re-energise and reinforce the alliances that have long been the strategic trump card of the democratic world . <p> But this is also an era of hard choices . What we ca n't afford is sentimentalism for an era that is past . In the race to innovate and adapt , there will be no salvation in wistful paeans to the old liberal international order . <h> Advertisement <p> There are several big swells in the ocean that have the potential to crest and come crashing down upon our heads in the year ahead . <p> The first , which remains the most important to the UK , is the future of Ukraine . We can be certain of some things in 2025 . One is that every actor , including presidents Zelensky and Putin , is gearing up for some sort of big political move and positioning themselves to maximise their leverage beforehand . <p> Yet the gulf between the general sense that a deal is coming and the creation of the conditions to bring it about remains huge . The problem with the idea of a " land for peace " deal , in which Ukraine cedes Russian-held territory in return for an end to hostilities , is that Putin 's primary target is not territory alone : it is the Ukrainian self-determination and sovereignty that would cement its place in the western orbit . <p> In the short run , then , the UK should be piling everything it can on to Ukraine 's side of the ledger in a " no regrets " strategy for 2025 , whether a viable peace negotiation emerges or not . Already , the prospect of putting some western troops in parts of Ukraine , albeit only in a training capacity or in the context of a ceasefire , is being actively considered in several European capitals . And there is now a live debate in both the EU and US Congress on how the hundreds of billions of dollars in frozen Russian assets , of which only the profit has been shaved off so far , could be used to strengthen the hand of Ukraine ahead of any talks . <p> If the UK wants to steer the Trump administration towards maintaining support for Ukraine , part of the answer is to show that Europe is willing to put more skin in the game itself . <h> Advertisement <h> Will Israel attack Iran ? <p> An anti-Israeli billboard looms larger in Tehran <p> ATTA KENARE/AFP/GETTY IMAGES <p> The second coming dilemma , and the one that may come at us fastest , is the next chapter in the Middle East conflict that has been raging since October 7 , 2023 , but has simmered away for a decade or more prior to that . <p> This war has many dimensions , including ongoing Houthi attacks on shipping , the future governance of Gaza and the attempt to find a stable equilibrium in post-Assad Syria , where Turkey is arguably the main beneficiary and Israel is already on the ground . <p> But the main event is likely to be what happens next between Israel and Iran , where the taboo on inter-state conflict -- direct attacks on each other 's countries -- has collapsed in the past 12 months . <p> Iran 's theocratic regime was by far the biggest geopolitical loser of 2024 . Its proxies and patsies , from Hamas to Hezbollah to Bashar al-Assad , have suffered a series of stunning reverses . Could it now accept a deal in which its nuclear ambitions are visibly and dramatically curtailed ? Or will it opt instead for a game of brinkmanship against an Israel that has shown , notably with its airstrikes in October , that it can hit the regime at its heart , damaging Iranian air defences in the process ? <p> With the arrival of Trump , Israel may now have a partner in the White House that is willing to back it in going further in exerting maximum pressure on Iran , potentially even targeting its nuclear capabilities . There is no playbook for how the UK would respond in such circumstances , but one can foresee a hard dilemma about whether to align with a ratcheting-up , or to try to sit it out . <h> Advertisement <h> The third dilemma <p> President Xi inspects troops this month in Macau , southern China <p> LI GANG/XINHUA/AP <p> The China challenge is rising back up the agenda just as Rachel Reeves prepares to travel to Beijing and the government seeks to improve its trading relations . Tensions have once again been rising in the South China Sea and over Taiwan , around which China conducted its largest military exercises in decades in early December . <p> For many years , national security officials have warned about a theoretical Taiwan invasion scenario taking place around 2027 , which is when Xi Jinping has ordered his military to be ready to take the island . But this single event horizon , the subject of a thousand war games , may not be the scenario that presents itself . <p> There is growing evidence that China could instead be adopting an incrementalist approach to change the facts on the ground in real time , asserting its control over territorial waters via its coast guard and navy , and gradually eroding Taiwanese sovereignty . <p> This type of asphyxiation strategy may seem less dramatic , but could very swiftly have a cascading effect on many other areas of our national security . Because Taiwan is the world 's main source of advanced semiconductors , which power our smartphones and laptops , this would deliver a shock to supply chains and the global economy that would make Ukraine pale by comparison . <p> Again , there is no playbook for Britain here . But there may be lessons from the case of Ukraine , when there was a divide in the G7 between those who wanted to advertise their economic deterrence measures before a potential invasion and those who thought such measures would be politically viable only once a Russian invasion actually took place . <h> Advertisement <p> Finally , there are those strategic challenges that governments like to bracket as " transnational " . Of these , migration and energy security are foremost . Policies on both will be defining issues at the next general election . <p> Yet , just as important , the government will also need to act fast to develop a new national security agenda for AI -- one that builds on but goes beyond the successful AI Safety Summit at Bletchley in 2023 -- if it is to stand any chance of keeping pace with the world . <h> The Trump factor <p> Donald Trump is Time magazine 's person of the year for 2024 <p> ALEX BRANDON/AP <p> The coming Trump administration is already brimming with a new elite of doges from the tech world who will surge efforts to win the race for technological primacy over China and spur American growth , unapologetically burning up a lot of rocket fuel and other energy sources on the way . <p> Meanwhile , the government is feeling its way towards a relatively modest reset with the EU , with Sir Keir Starmer establishing a new Whitehall unit to strengthen ties with the Continent . But this could be complicated by the prospect of a new form of 21st-century trade deal with the US . <p> There are two views in the US of how Trump 's international economic policy might play out . One version is a zero-sum and brutal use of tariffs to correct trade deficits and give a short-term fillip to domestic manufacturing . <h> Advertisement <p> But the other nascent proposition , seemingly favoured by Trump 's treasury secretary nominee Scott Bessent , is that America could create something like a US-led economic and security commons , bringing close allies such as the UK and Australia closer to its orbit in areas like tech regulation . <p> If the latter approach begins to crystallise , it will be difficult for Starmer 's government to resist the advances of the American grizzly bear . <p> The prize would be considerable , but a price will be exacted . <p> Voters expect Sir Keir Starmer to be an active part of the new world , John Bew writes <p> ANDY RAIN/EPA <p> Reaching a favourable deal with the US will not be possible if the UK diverges significantly on issues like China or indeed Israel , the issue on which all elements of the Trump administration are united and where the distance between London and Washington may be most pronounced . <p> And what would it mean for the EU reset if the UK had a sweetheart deal with the US , in which it was excluded from tariffs crashing down on the rest of Europe ? <p> The electorate will expect the government to be active participants in this new world , rather than passive recipients of whatever it throws upon our shores . Could Starmer be the first leader to see President Trump in 2025 , perhaps even before his inauguration , with a bold proposition for how the US-UK relationship could be bolstered on trade and security ? <p> There is a lot to be said for first-mover advantage in foreign policy . But the path ahead requires imagination , boldness , risk-taking and a willingness to accept difficult trade-offs that would strain any government , particularly one dealing with sclerotic growth . <p> One thing is for certain , though , in the era of grizzly bears , tech pioneers and new frontiers : playing possum wo n't do . <p> John Bew is professor of history and foreign policy at King 's College London . He was foreign policy adviser to No 10 for five years

Their common scourges were typhus , smallpox , tuberculosis , anthrax , scabies and syphilis -- all untreatable at the time . And then there was the plague . <p> The plague tore up the foundations of society and paved the way for dramatic economic , political and social change <p> Arriving at the ports of Venice , Pisa and Marseilles in 1347 , shipboard rats carrying the Yersinia Pestis bacterium disbursed the bubonic plague in Europe . By legend , the Mongol Jani Beg , leader of the Golden Horde , catapulted plague-infected bodies into the city . @@119381250 <h> The UK 's stance on Israel is about to become way more complicated <p> Starmer and Lammy can not hope that the questions will only last a few more months <p> December 28 , 2024 7:00 am <p> The Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary will be asked repeatedly to comment on US-Israel policy with each new utterance from President Trump ( Photo : Saul Loeb/AFP ) <p> cancel **31;843;TOOLONG Share bookmark Save <p> share cancel **34;876;TOOLONG <p> " Israel is only getting started " is not a statement that would automatically spark joy in UK government ministers who are still trying to work out how to relate to Benjamin Netanyahu . Just days ago , Keir Starmer said in his Christmas message that he was particularly hoping for peace in the Middle East . Israel 's strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen suggest that wish is n't coming true any time soon . As one conflict closes , another opens up . <p> And yet as well as at least notionally supporting Israel 's right to defend herself against terrorists who want to eliminate the Jewish state , the UK also has an interest in tackling the Houthi rebels . They are not just a threat to Israel or the wider region , but also to this country , which is why the UK and US took part in strikes against the Iranian-backed group earlier this year . <p> The difference , of course , now is that Israel is the country on the attack , and the international narrative currently is that an intervention from Israel is bad , even if the same action by other countries was Ok . The Israeli action to dismantle Syria 's chemical weapons capability after the fall of the Assad regime was not seen as a positive , but as a potential escalation in the region . <p> Netanyahu has specifically pointed to what happened in Syria , along with the conflict with Hamas and Hezbollah , as a reason for pursuing the Houthis . " As I said , Hamas learned , Hezbollah learned , and Syria learned , " he said , adding : " The Houthis will learn too . " Hamas and Hezbollah have " learned " in part through the targeting of their leaders by the IDF . But the Houthis are not an easy force to defeat : Saudi Arabia has also been trying to fight them for years . This suggests another protracted conflict when Israel is now into its 15th month of fighting Hamas following the 7 October atrocities . Once again , the UK will have to work out how to talk about this conflict . <p> There will be pressure when Parliament returns to criticise the retraction of a US report which warned that a " famine scenario " was unfolding in Gaza . The word " famine " is almost as hotly contested as the word " genocide " , something pro-Palestinian Labour MPs want the UK Government to say is happening in Gaza . Starmer has refused to do this . Yemen itself was an extremely sensitive topic within Labour when Jeremy Corbyn was leader , and the involvement of Israel threatens to reignite those political tensions . <p> Complicating matters is the fact that Keir Starmer and David Lammy want to work constructively with the incoming Trump administration , which will expect a much more full-throated support of Israel than the UK has offered for a while . The Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary will be asked repeatedly to comment on US-Israel policy with each new utterance from President Trump . <p> Working out how to balance those differences is going to be one of the early jobs of the new ambassador to Washington , Peter Mandelson . <p> Mandelson has compared calls to back a ceasefire in Gaza to suggestions that the UK should have done nothing to dismantle the IRA during the Troubles . He is not the only senior Labour figure to make parallels between Northern Ireland and the Middle East : Starmer himself has drawn on his own experience of working with the Police Service of Northern Ireland in the 2000s . <p> He has now tasked Lammy with trying to copy some of the work in the peace process there , with an international summit in London early in the new year , where civil society organisations building dialogue between Israelis and Palestinians will discuss how to create a lasting peace and move closer to a two-state solution . <p> The chances of that solution still seem pretty far off at present : hopes before Christmas of a ceasefire in the conflict with Hamas turned to naught , and Netanyahu suggested they were just rumours spread to weaken Israel 's position . Until there is a deal which not only leads to the release of the remaining hostages , but also leaves Israel confident that Hamas is not in power in Gaza and can not continue to threaten Israelis ' security , then a ceasefire is not possible . <p> There are a lot of " untils " in this column , which means Starmer and Lammy can not hope that the questions about their stance on Israel will only last a few more months . As Netanyahu said , those questions are only just starting .

As 2024 ends , regional wars are becoming increasingly intertwined between emerging coalitions . A growing cabal of autocrats are increasingly seeing the benefit of collaborating on drones , intelligence , sanctions-busting and deploying troops in service of each other 's wars . <p> Israel and Iran have traded direct missile attacks ( as have Israel and the Houthis who have attacked international shipping in the Red Sea ) . The reaction to the murderous attacks of October 7 2023 has devastated Gaza , and expanded to a war in Lebanon . A stretched Russia and Iran were unable to prevent the fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria , as they had in 2015 . In Europe , North Korean troops have been deployed to fight alongside Russian troops attempting to retake Russian land that Ukraine has seized , while western weapons are being used to hit targets in Russia . Russia 's " grey zone " war has continued to spread across Europe with increasingly brazen attacks . Warfare is no longer restricted to the battlefield . <p> While the incoming US president has vowed to end the Ukraine war in a day , the spreading of conflict looks set to continue in 2025 . Indeed , the return of Trump could see an explosive acceleration of the chain reaction . <p> If Trump is successful in abruptly ending the war in Ukraine , it could hasten the beginning of a new one . If Ukrainian land is ceded to Russia without concrete security guarantees , such as Nato membership , this would weaken long-term European security , erode US credibility as an ally and embolden Russia and other states with long-held territorial ambitions . This includes China 's ambitions of reunification with Taiwan . Economic challenges within China , leading to internal instability , could change president Xi 's timelines for achieving this ambition . <p> In 2025 , Israel will run out of things to destroy in Gaza . A ceasefire is possible in the near future , with Benjamin Netanyahu providing Trump with a foreign policy win in exchange for support against Iran . Trump 's social media suggests the return of the Israeli hostages will be a priority -- but he will do nothing to ease the pain of a generation of Gazans who have lost loved ones . This will leave a fertile recruiting ground for those seeking violent revenge . <p> A fragile ceasefire with Hezbollah does n't mean an easing of tensions with Iran . Removing Hezbollah 's offensive capabilities was always a part of a wider Israeli plan to deal with Iran . If Trump gives Netanyahu the green light to attack the Iranian nuclear programme , he will have to carefully manage his relationship with Putin . Russia has deepened its relationship with Iran . However , Trump and Putin will feel they can do business : US concessions over Ukraine given in exchange for Russian concessions over Iran . <p> As for China , it is walking a delicate line between fostering an anti-US military partnership between Russia , North Korea and Iran , and avoiding sanctions and the disapproval of key economic partners . Trump has announced that he will increase tariffs on China by 10% in January . Many expect an escalating trade war as Trump uses tariffs as a weapon of diplomacy . <p> Trump 's disruptive and unpredictable approach could have its uses . Yet his inconsistency , aversion to multilateral approaches and vulnerability to flattery will undermine his pursuit of " peace through strength " . Next year may be defined as much by what Trump does n't do , as by what he does . <p> The philosopher John Gray believes Trump 's return " ... marks a historic turning point , comparable in its geopolitical consequences with the Soviet collapse : the definitive end of a liberal world order . With regime change in the US , countries that relied on American protection face an unavoidable choice : arm and defend themselves , or else make peace with the rising authoritarian powers . " <p> America remains an economic superpower at the centre of AI development , which has the potential to create exponential economic growth ( albeit with accompanying social upheaval ) . Trump , however , wants to be free to focus on the primacy of US economic interests , not the primacy of western ideals . His isolationist approach will weaken America 's already waning position . <p> Many in the global south have learned the lesson of Afghanistan , Libya and Syria : do n't trust western coalitions to stand up for the ideals they claim to hold . Along with Burkina Faso , Mali , Somalia and Sudan , these countries are again becoming safe havens for extremism , which are likely to fuel the revival of terrorist networks . While the fall of Assad is being rightly celebrated , 2025 could see Syria descend into the same chaos that engulfed Libya after the fall of Colonel Gaddafi . When ideologically diverse groups , united by a single objective , achieve their goal , what they have in common becomes less than their differences . But even if the dominant rebel group in the push to Damascus , Hayat Tahrir al-Sham , which emerged from al-Qaida , manages to hold together a new Syrian government , the risk of Syria becoming an Islamist terrorist safe haven remains . <p> Israel is already taking steps to minimise this risk by targeting weapons factories and other elements of Syria 's military infrastructure as well as seizing strategic land . Dormant conflicts are awakening . <p> The revival of terror networks highlights another theme of 2025 : turning your back on the world wo n't stop it coming to you . A trade war between the US and China will affect the cost of living for all of us . <p> Xi will hope Trump 's isolationist " America First " will further the emergence of a China-centred alternative to the western-dominated financial system . Through state investment and espionage , China is attempting to surpass the west 's technological and military capabilities . Through the Belt and Road Initiative and its successor , the Global Development Initiative , China has spread both debt and the tools for autocracy across the global south , in exchange for natural resources and trade deals . <p> Xi 's vision discards the idea of alliances based on universal values in favour of non-binding partnerships predicated on common interests . This is not dissimilar to Trump 's view -- the tension between the two is over who has primacy in this new world of " equals " . <p> Wars tend to concentrate at times when power is transitioning . The old system benefited the west and lifted many in the global south out of poverty , yet it has also perpetuated inequality , and western foreign policy has regularly been hypocritical . <p> What the new order will be is not yet determined . As others try to turn their back on the world or focus on the primacy of their own interests , our government must build new coalitions and institutions to ensure that we avoid losing the international norms we value . @@119392277 <h> We can not give in to defeatism as Trump 's toxic influence poisons the global well <h> Do n't give in to defeatism as Trump 's toxicity poisons the global well <p> SO bigly has the world changed in the last eight years -- so battered into submission have we been by the pandemic , conflicts , climate change and the rise of the right -- it is difficult to recall the shock of Donald Trump 's first election victory , or to summon up the spirit of resistance that led millions to protest in the days after his 2017 inauguration . <p> Back then , everything the new president did -- every rambling speech , every late-night tweet , every on-the-hoof policy announcement -- was met with an outpouring of anger and defiance that seems touchingly naive from today 's more jaded standpoint . <p> This time , there is even more reason to worry . Now , Trump is a convicted felon , bankrolled by Elon Musk , who bought a social media platform to peddle misinformation on his behalf . <p> He has greater control over Washington : the Republicans ' Senate majority is slightly bigger , the Supreme Court is stacked in his favour , and he has offloaded any party stalwarts unwilling to sign up to his Make America Great Again ( MAGA ) agenda . <p> Meanwhile , he is cosying up to the two world leaders -- Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu -- responsible for the worst ( and potentially globally consequential ) acts of aggression so far this century . <p> Yet , we have become so inured to the corruption and extremism at the heart of his project that a frenzy of antagonistic season-of-badwill posts -- in which he criticised Justin Trudeau and lashed out at " radical left lunatics " -- caused barely a ripple of consternation . <p> Nowadays , Trump can threaten to annex Canada , buy Greenland and retake the Panama Canal , and the response is little more than a raised eyebrow and an " och , there he goes again " shrug of the shoulders . <p> It 's not that people are n't scared , it 's that the focus is less on fighting the machine than on self-preservation , and the shoring up of positions . Some are acting cynically . <p> Naughty list BIG corporations -- including a few which pledged to cut Trump off after the 2021 Capitol riot -- have been currying favour by donating millions to his inaugural fund ( he 's said to be keeping a naughty list of those who do n't ) . <p> Others , like the universities urging international students to return early from their winter breaks in case of a fresh Muslim travel ban , are acting out of desperation and in the hopes of protecting their most vulnerable from the predicted consequences of Trump 's second term . <p> There 's a weariness and a sort of defeatism in the air . The 2017 Muslim travel ban sparked ad hoc protests at airports , while Trump 's rhetoric on reproductive issues led to large-scale women 's marches in cities across the world . <p> I joined the Edinburgh women 's march and the one a year or so later in protest against his state visit to the UK . But they were exercises in futility . <p> Trump was still feted by the Queen and Theresa May . Roe v Wade was still overturned . If 77 million Americans do n't care that a jury of their peers found their president liable for sexual abuse ( if they do n't care that he is appointing anti-vaxxers and sexual abusers to his administration ) , then what difference is waving a placard on the other side of the Atlantic going to make ? <p> The events of the last few years , in the US and elsewhere , have brought a kind of learned helplessness . When Russia invaded Ukraine , there was an initial pulling together -- sending donations , and then taking in refugees -- and the UK Government has continued to provide money and weaponry ( as it absolutely should ) . <p> But two years on , people are still dying , and Putin can launch a Christmas Day attack on the country 's energy infrastructure with impunity . <p> Then , there is the horror of watching the genocide in Gaza unfold in real time , while world leaders -- in hock to Netanyahu -- utter their weasel words . Petitions are ignored , protesters often written off as anti-Semites . <p> There appears to be nothing we can do to stop our government arming Israel or to convince it to introduce the kind of sweeping trade sanctions which helped to end apartheid in South Africa . Trump 's presidency has done nothing to assuage public concerns . <p> If he can -- as he has promised -- bring an end to the Ukrainian conflict , it is likely to be at the expense of Ukraine ( and with what long-term consequences for Europe , one wonders ? ) . <p> As for Gaza , in his first term , Trump moved the US Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem , and he has stuffed his new administration full of pro-Israeli hawks , so there 's scarcely cause for optimism there either . <p> Disconnect OUR impotence in the face of political intransigence -- combined with the all-pervasive nature of social media -- is leading otherwise engaged people to disconnect . <p> A recent Associated Press/NORC poll suggested 65% of American adults wanted to limit their consumption of news about politics and the government . I feel it too : that growing reluctance to watch the TV footage or scroll through my feeds because what 's the point in being informed if you ca n't change a single damn thing ? <p> So , we are silenced by our powerlessness , but also by a fear of exacerbating the situation . One of the neatest tricks the right has pulled off is to make those of us who are angry about Donald Trump responsible for his rise . It was , so the theory goes , the hysteria of " woke elites " that alienated the working classes . It 's neat because it 's partly true . <p> We should have grasped that decades of marginalisation would make certain sections of society more susceptible to the siren song of demagogues . We should have understood more and condemned less . <p> But it 's also convenient because " woke elites " are easily guilt-tripped , and because their decision to shut up and opt out allows Trump 's lies and toxicity to go unchallenged . <p> After his election in November , Rebecca Solnit -- a woman very often dismissed as both " woke " and " elite " -- reminded us of the need to keep going , or at least of the need not to quit . Quoting the LGBT historian Gerard Koskovich , she described succumbing to despair as a kind of complicity . <p> This is going to be particularly relevant to those of us in the UK in the coming year as we face up to a new threat from Nigel Farage 's Reform Party . Last week , the party announced it now has over 132,000 members -- more than the Conservatives -- and declared itself the new Opposition . <p> Some polls have suggested the party could win 1,000 councillors between now and the next General Election , taking votes from both the Tories and Labour . <p> Meanwhile , in Scotland too , its popularity is increasing . Reform took 7% of the vote north of the Border in the General Election in July , overtaking the Conservatives in 25 seats , despite very little campaigning or party infrastructure . And the Scottish Parliament 's system of proportional representation is likely to benefit the party in the 2026 Holyrood election . <p> This is , in other words , no time to give up ; to accept that we are doomed ; to surrender to the apparent inexorability of dark forces . <p> Daunting prospects <p> THERE is work to be done : at home and abroad . Heading into January , with so much at stake , is daunting . The prospect of another four years of Trump is bleak . <p> But wallowing in the disappointment of Kamala Harris 's defeat gets us nowhere ( and in any case let 's not kid ourselves the Democrats would have offered any kind of global panacea ) . <p> If the scale of the world 's problems has a paralysing effect , then we could focus on those small things that are in our gift : cleaving to our principles ; supporting those around us ; contributing to our communities ; calling out misinformation , but without laying blame . <p> Such actions may not alter the course of history , but there 's a dignity in remaining true to yourself in the face of attempts to erase you . We should show , not tell . <p> Live the way we 'd like the world to be . @@119392287 <h> Why a truly turbulent year awaits the world in 2025 <h> Why a truly turbulent year awaits the world in 2025 <p> Former U.S. President Donald Trump enters Erie Insurance Arena for a political rally while campaigning for the GOP nomination . Photo by Jeff Swensen/Getty Images ) . <p> The past 12 months have seen the globe rocked by conflicts and major shifts in power , but as the new year beckons , Foreign Editor David Pratt runs the rule over what might lie head <p> As the old saying goes , prediction is hard , especially if it 's about the future . Most foreign affairs writers , analysts and correspondents will identify with that age old maxim and agree that crystal ball gazing over major world stories is something of a mugs game . <p> This past year 2024 has been a point in case , for what a surprising , seismic , and turbulent year it has been on the world stage . <p> To name but just a few of the stories that have shaped the past 12 months , firstly there was Donald Trump 's incredible sweeping victory in the US presidential election . Incumbent Joe Biden was not the only one to lose out either , as more than 40 per cent of the planet 's population went to the polls in 2024 , many punishing politicians in power in the mother of all election years . <p> Then there was the shift in momentum to Russia in the third year of the war in Ukraine . And last but far from least , profound upheaval even by Middle East standards that saw the region undergo a geopolitical relandscaping culminating with the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad 's decades long authoritarian rule in Syria . <p> Yes , making predictions for the year ahead is fraught with pitfalls , but that never stops us from trying to read the runes , such is the almost universal obsession with gaining a ' window ' on the world in which we live and its impact on all our lives no matter how far-flung and removed events might appear to be . <p> It 's in that spirit then that I thought it at least a useful exercise in this last Sunday edition of 2024 , to flag up a few global news themes worth keeping an eye on in 2025 . <p> What follows is far from being a ' definitive ' or ' correct ' list of those stories or themes likely to shape the coming year , and I should stress is a purely personal take . But without doubt , each of these themes will resonate over next twelve months and beyond - so here we go . <p> Trump 's policy coherence will be as elusive as ever <p> Few would disagree that Donald Trump 's electoral victory was the political pinnacle of last year . As he takes office again on January 20 , so the impact of his presidency will be felt in a number of ways in terms of foreign policy . His appointments to date of key staff provide some of the clues as to what we can expect - or do they ? <p> Many international affairs experts , among them Karin von Hippel , director of the Royal United Services Institute ( RUSI ) in London , believe that Trump 's pick n mix approach is more about surrounding himself with loyalists rather than real strategic forward thinking . <p> " It 's almost like what he 's doing with his appointments is like a Jackson Pollock painting . He 's just throwing everything at the wall , throwing a lot of crazy characters at the wall in hopes that some of those guys will get through , " observed von Hippel recently in an assessment some art historians might feel an unfair comparison with the creative thinking behind the great American abstract expressionist painter 's method of working . <p> But levity aside , the 47th US president will be less constrained than the 45th albeit they are the same person . This ' less ' constrained Trump cuts both ways , acting I believe both as a force for good and one that is bad . Knowing this , countries around the world are already bracing for his impact . <p> Where I believe Trump can act as force for good is in his long established capacity to shake things up . On the right day this can result in a positive refocusing of minds that have become complacent or entrenched . <p> Top of Trump 's list will be Washington 's fraught , geopolitical relations with Russia and China . Watch out for him attempting a reset of relations with both , especially with his counterpart Vladimir Putin , which in turn could bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table to discuss terms of a peace deal . <p> Europe here must ensure it has both a seat and voice at the table to ensure that its clout is not seriously undermined and Ukraine hung out to dry diplomatically . <p> In Trump 's eyes , brokering this could mean a land-for-peace agreement with security guarantees for Ukraine in Europe stopping short of NATO membership . <p> As for China , the US president-elect knows that this year will be crucial for China 's sluggish economy . To that end , Trump might be tempted to turn the screw through tariffs but again look out for a deal here too . <p> Much will depend on which of Trump 's character traits comes to the fore and the degree of influence some national security hardliners like Mike Waltz , Marco Rubio and others within his administration bring to bear . We might see the Trump who likes to do big deals with strong leaders or the competitive Trump who still feels cheated by China on Covid and the bilateral trade deal during his last term in the White House . <p> I 'll stick my neck out here and say that Beijing may be inclined to negotiate a new agreement with Trump similar to the one made just before Covid , to stabilise its relationship with the US and buy time for internal reforms . Trump the force for good might seem like a strange call , but I stress again the unpredictable nature of his policy implementation means it could cut both ways . <p> As someone who has spent a substantial part of my four decade long foreign affairs reporting career covering the Middle East , rarely in that time could I have imagined a chain of events like those that unfolded last year in the wake of the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 . That almost all these bitter and bloody events have their festering roots going back much longer goes without saying , but what now lies ahead for the region in 2025 and beyond ? <p> To begin with Gaza , the outlook for the foreseeable future for Palestinians is I believe as bleak as ever . <p> Roughly 15 months into Israel 's war on Gaza , which both Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have concluded constitutes a genocide , 2025 I believe will see Israel establish a full presence in the north of the coastal enclave . Elsewhere in Gaza the suffering will continue as Israeli forces double down on what remains of Hamas . In the occupied West Bank meanwhile keep an eye on what will be accelerated Israeli settlement growth , as per far right ultranationalist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich 's ' Decisive Plan , ' which was published in 2017 . As one Israeli newspaper commentator recently observed , with settlers lining up to get into Gaza and Lebanon , " it 's getting harder to push back against talk of Israeli empire-building . " <p> This is almost certain to trigger new rounds of violence , though Israel in 2025 will continue to use what it sees as a ' golden ' opportunity , to neutralise Tehran 's so called ' axis of resistance , ' with the Houthis in Yemen now firmly in its crosshairs . Looking to 2025 , one of the potential flashpoints in the region will be a resumption of hostilities between Tehran and Tel Aviv . <p> Elsewhere in the region watch out for the Syrian ' honeymoon ' period after Assad 's ouster unravelling and fractures opening up . The intervention of outside actors in post-Assad Syria will have a major impact on what happens next . In 2025 many external players will seek to influence Syria 's vulnerable transition in ways that serve their own interests . Turkey especially is worth monitoring as it seeks to use its rebel proxies in Syria to eliminate any threat from Kurdish aspirations for independence . As the New Arab online magazine rightly recently pointed out , as Tehran 's grip on the region loosens , the stage is set for Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan to potentially fill the vacuum and redefine the regional order . <p> Ukrainian firefighters work to extinguish a fire at the site of a drone attack on industrial facilities in Kharkiv ( Photo by SERGEY BOBOK / AFP ) <p> The year of make or break for Ukraine <p> Whatever happens in 2025 it will prove a crucial year for Russia 's war in Ukraine . <p> Trump has promised to end the conflict there , but the fact remains that the Ukrainian and Russian visions of a settlement differ wildly , and Russian President Vladimir Putin has shown little interest in serious negotiations . <p> But watch out nevertheless for Trump attempting to broker an agreement . Last month the Wall Street Journal ( WSJ ) citing policy advisers close to Trump , reported that they were considering offering a deal whereby the current fighting lines would be frozen - cementing Russia 's seizure of roughly 20% of Ukraine -and forcing Ukraine to temporarily suspend its quest to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation ( NATO ) . <p> According to the WSJ , one idea proposed by Trump 's transition team and up until then not previously reported , would involve Kyiv promising not to join NATO for at least 20 years . The US meantime would continue to provide weapons supplies to deter a future Russian attack and the frontline would essentially lock in place and both sides agree to an 800-mile demilitarised zone . <p> Highlighting the tricky question of who would police such a zone , the WSJ cited a Trump adviser insisting that whoever did it , they would certainly not be American military or part of a US-funded international body , such as the United Nations <p> " We can do training and other support but the barrel of the gun is going to be European , " a member of Trump 's team said . " We are not sending American men and women to uphold peace in Ukraine . And we are not paying for it . Get the Poles , Germans , British and French to do it , " the newspaper quoted the adviser as saying bluntly . <p> Whether such a deal and frozen conflict comes so fruition in 2025 remains to be seen , but there is a real sense that one way or another the coming year could be a make or break one for Ukraine . <p> A boy waves a flag during a mourning demonstration in the Mezzah district on December 27 , 2024 in Damascus , Syria <p> UK will have to decide is it Europe or America ? <p> In 2025 Trump 's sweeping victory will affect everything from immigration and defence to economics , trade and alliances . His " America First " policy will have friends and foes alike questioning the solidity of America 's alliances . This could lead to geopolitical realignments and heightened tensions . <p> Right now , Europe itself is politically vulnerable with Germany , under Olaf Scholz tearing itself apart and France 's minority government surviving at the behest of the far-right leader Marine Le Pen . <p> As this weakened Europe struggles to forge a common front , Trump will seek to exploit this and if America is to continue to back Europe , the US president will want something tangible in return , whether on trade , military contracts or direct payments . <p> Few issues will test this common European front more than that of Trump 's threat of imposing trade tariffs , which has already stimulated an internal debate in Europe on how to respond . <p> In the coming year watch out for Sir Keir Starmer 's government struggling to balance relations with the US and Europe . Speaking earlier this month Starmer " utterly rejected " the idea that the UK must choose between the US and Europe arguing that it is in the national interest to work with both . <p> If Trump follows through on his announced plans to impose tariffs on the US 's trade partners , then he could pressure the UK to effectively pick sides between America and the European Union ( EU ) . <p> Starmer has said that the UK would " never turn away " from its relationship with the US , despite the difficulties the new administration could pose , as it had been the " cornerstone " of security and prosperity for over a century . <p> Polling published this month by the European Council on Foreign Relations , showed that right across Europe voters prefer more Europe to more Trump . The question now is whether if put to the test Starmer 's government thinks the same if forced to decide on going with Europe or Trump 's America . <p> Other stories to watch out for <p> While much of the focus in terms of foreign stories in 2025 will stem from Trump , and the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East , other major events should also be on our radar . Among other more wild card predictions here are a few to add to the watchlist . <p> First up , the return of geopolitical competition will further intensify in the shape of what has been called the ' axis of autocracies , ' ' the axis of upheaval ' and the ' quartet of chaos ' or to put this another way the growing cooperation between China , Russia , Iran , and North Korea . Once again Trump 's administration could have a major impact on how this develops - or not . <p> Watch out too for the growing constitutional crisis brewing in Tbilisi , Georgia , which as I write will reach boiling point as the newly elected , far-right pro-Russian President Mikheil Kavelashvili is inaugurated today Dec. 29 . It could well be a volatile year in Georgia . <p> Farther afield , twenty months into a civil war , the world 's biggest humanitarian crisis in Sudan is almost certain to get worse as the country continues to slide into a widening famine crisis with food stocks likely to be exhausted ahead of the usual lean season . This underreported story is one that should concern us all and will sadly make headlines for all the wrong reasons in 2025 . <p> In Asia meanwhile , 2025 could well signal the end of the junta in Myanmar much as 2024 saw the overthrow of Assad 's ' regime in Syria . Declining morale within the army , failure to recruit new soldiers and loss of support from major backers like Russia , has seen opposition gains that could well see the bottom fall out of the junta . <p> In short , if 2024 saw turbulent times then so too does the year ahead look set to be a rocky one . Whatever occurs , here 's hoping for more peace on the horizon . <h> Why are you making commenting on The Herald only available to subscribers ? <p> It should have been a safe space for informed debate , somewhere for readers to discuss issues around the biggest stories of the day , but all too often the below the line comments on most websites have become bogged down by off-topic discussions and abuse . <p> heraldscotland.com is tackling this problem by allowing only subscribers to comment . <p> We are doing this to improve the experience for our loyal readers and we believe it will reduce the ability of trolls and troublemakers , who occasionally find their way onto our site , to abuse our journalists and readers . @@119392549 <p> The Halo Trust works around the world clearing land contaminated after war ( Image : Jonathan Buckmaster ) <p> Boats run by criminal gangs . Refugees stuck in expensive hotels . It 's easy to see why many people want the government to stop illegal migration . <p> As a retired Major General who runs one of Britain 's largest overseas charities , I can see a way to address the issue . <p> Rather than pay billions to keep refugees in hotels , the UK could invest more in programmes to help people stay closer to their homes in safety . <p> The HALO Trust was founded in Afghanistan in 1988 . We are famous for destroying landmines - thanks to Princess Diana , who visited us in Angola in 1997 . <p> But we destroy far more than landmines . We clear unexploded bombs and rockets . And we help secure rifles , pistols , and bullets . In short , we take care of anything that goes bang . How does this relate to the small boats crisis ? <p> Recent statistics tell us that the largest group of illegal migrants coming to the UK is from Afghanistan . Many come here because life is too dangerous for them at home . <p> Landmines and other explosives prevent farmers from growing crops and stop children walking safely to school . What if they did n't have to come here in the first place ? <p> Life in Afghanistan today is tough , particularly for women and girls , who are denied the most basic rights . Deadly landmines , however , are indiscriminate and blight the country for everyone . <p> If you remove these explosives , people can live in safety in their own country , without risking their lives at sea in search of a better future . <p> I have seen entire towns built on former battlegrounds or minefields in Afghanistan . I have talked to displaced Afghan families who have built new homes on land we have cleared of landmines . But handing over safe , cleared land is not enough . People also need livelihoods . <p> The HALO Trust was founded by two former Scottish soldiers who trained local people in Afghanistan to clear landmines to a professional standard . They rightly thought that employing locals was a better idea than paying high wages for Western military personnel to do the same thing . <p> Today , HALO has 12,000 highly trained women and men working in nearly 30 countries . In Afghanistan alone , we employ over 2000 staff . Each employee has about 20 dependents reliant on their salary . <p> So that 's well over 40,000 people able to stay in Afghanistan , supported by a decent local wage . But it does n't end there : we calculate that four million Afghans make a living on land made safe by HALO . <p> The British taxpayer has helped these Afghan families build a life in Afghanistan , rather than risking their lives on illegal boats or subsisting in limbo in hotels in British seaside resorts . <p> It costs the government just ? 2million a year to help HALO support over 40,000 Afghans and keep many , many more safely at home . Compare that sum to the millions of pounds Britain spends every day on housing Afghans here . <p> It 's a similar story for Syria , Iraq , and Libya , where HALO also works . And with Gaza under rubble and over a million people already displaced inside Lebanon , we know that more refugees will want to be on the move . <p> The Labour government has an opportunity to re-frame overseas aid as a form of defence , rather than altruism or ' woke tokenism ' . <p> By funding organisations like HALO to clear up after conflict , Sir Keir Starmer has a thrifty and humane solution that helps tackle migration at source . <p> You can find out more and support The Halo Trust 's life-saving work here . 
@@119392680 <h> From climate denial to gothic movies to ' treat culture ' ... what to expect in 2025 <p> Full steam ahead : from left , Nigel Farage , David Bowie , Leigh Bowery , a character from Memoir of a Snail and Liam Gallagher.Composite : Hollie Adams/Reuters , The Hartnett Archive , Sipa Press/Rex , film still , Andrew Benge/Redferns <h> Foreign affairs <p> The only thing that can be predicted with absolute certainty about Donald Trump 's second term as US president is that it will be unpredictable . Trump does not really know what he wants to do on a range of issues . He talks a good game , which is how he got re-elected . But he often seems to decide policy on the basis of what the last person he spoke to told him . Is he serious about mobilising the military to carry out mass deportations of " illegal " migrants ? Will he use the justice department to hunt down political enemies and media critics ? Will he impose sweeping tariffs on foreign imports and trigger a global trade war ? Or will he act with greater circumspection , using these threats as bargaining tools ? Who knows ? He does n't yet . <p> In Ukraine , it 's a fairly safe bet that some form of negotiations or talks about negotiations to halt , if not end , the war with Russia will begin . European governments appear to be preparing for a Trump-led effort to force a reluctant Kyiv to the table , with the price of peace being territorial concessions involving Crimea and the large chunk of eastern Ukraine currently under Moscow 's control . Any such deal may be preceded by a ceasefire and the separation of opposing forces along a line of control or demilitarised zone . Ukraine will want security guarantees against future attack . Vladimir Putin will want assurances Ukraine will not join Nato . A lot could go wrong . Amid rising tensions between Russia and the west at the year 's close , it remains possible the conflict will expand into a wider European war . <p> It 's hard to believe that things could get any worse in Gaza and the Palestinian territories than they were in 2024 -- but they could , and probably will . It can be assumed that an elusive ceasefire in Gaza will eventually be agreed , but at a high cost . It may leave hundreds of thousands of Palestinians permanently dispossessed and homeless , and Israeli forces occupying a large area of northern Gaza . Emboldened by Trump 's re-election , the hard-right Netanyahu coalition may move to annex much of the West Bank in pursuit of a " Greater Israel " . Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon , having taken a beating , will be hard-put to stop it . So , too , will the international courts . Joe Biden 's hopes of a two-state solution and a wider Middle East settlement will lie in ashes along with his presidency . Simon Tisdall <h> Technology <p> A few themes will dominate the year . The first is the AI bubble into which the tech giants have been pumping unconscionable sums of money with , at the moment , no conceivable or proportionate return . The two big questions then are : when will it burst -- and when it does , what will be the consequences ? Investors will lose their shirts , as usual , but the impact will be more significant than the dotcom bust in 2000 , and stock markets will feel it first , as tech stocks have a disproportionate impact on the key indices . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> There will also be a consummation of the shotgun marriage between the tech industry and US politics . From now on they will be inextricably mixed -- as the tech moguls intuited when they decided to endorse Trump . Elon Musk and X will thrive , as will Trump 's Truth Social . Bluesky will become the last redoubt of liberalism . And LinkedIn will follow the corporate herd . It 's not clear how Trump will vent his spite against Meta , but he will . The company may eventually decide that it will have to split into two entities : Meta US , which conforms to Trumpian decrees , and Meta EU , which can operate within EU jurisdiction and elsewhere . <p> As far as Google is concerned , just about the only Biden initiative the US justice department will continue is the antitrust case against Google . This will end only when the company is forced to divest itself of Chrome ( and maybe some other bits too ) . Elsewhere on the regulatory front , the Federal Communications Commission ( FCC ) , under the chairmanship of Brendan Carr , will pursue fruitless attempts to amend Section 230 of the 1996 Telecommunications Act to bring social media under the governmental heel . Carr also has fantasies about trying to ensure the first amendment protects only speech that is congenial to the Maga regime . <p> Under Trump , ? cryptocurrencies will be liberated from the fear of oversight by government authorities , with societal consequences that will make current levels of grift and fraud in the industry look like a Victorian tea party . <p> And finally , Global Britain will remain an interested but impotent onlooker on all of the above . John Naughton <h> Food <p> Food in 2025 will become like everything else in 2025 : more extreme . There will be a ? superabundance of everything you like and everything you hate . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> YouTube channel TopJaw will be supplanted by an AI-generated definitive list of the " world 's best things " updated every hour and delivered in an editing style designed to be medically addictive . Simultaneously , the urge to experience individuality in an age of conformity will see an upsurge in those seeking out more organic recommendations from micro-influencers , and nano-influencers , and micro-nano-influencers ( or , as they used to be known , " other people " ) . <p> People will eat more -- ? queueing outside whichever unsuspecting neighbourhood eatery has been anointed/cursed by the latest viral TikTok trend , a la Queen 's Wood Cafe in London ( although they 'll also , inexplicably , eternally , continue queueing outside The Breakfast Club , for reasons unknown to modern science ) . They 'll also eat less -- with the cost of living continuing to encroach from one side and the march of Ozempic on the other . <p> Restaurants will somehow become more prohibitively expensive and more inaccessibly fully booked . Burgers will continue to become more smashed ( see Supernova ) and students will continue to become less smashed . We will crawl , terrifyingly , towards the era of the ? 10 pint . <p> Everything will become fermented , raw , biodynamic , locally sourced , artisanal , vegan and three new things none of us have heard of yet but which will be a core part of our identities by March and pass ? by August . Consumers will know more than ever , but be beset by the perennial worry that they 're lagging behind on whatever the latest fad is , or was , or might be . <p> And perhaps there are predictions to be made about things that wo n't change . Tradition still means something in London 's restaurants . Max Olesker <h> Culture <p> It is hard to ignore an exhibitionist , but it will be harder than usual in 2025 as a string of cultural figures with main ? character energy are placed centre stage . In February , Tate Modern kicks off its 25th anniversary year with a salute to the late Leigh Bowery , the influential clubber , designer , muse and performance artist of 1980s London . Bowery arrived from Melbourne , Australia , and his eccentric outfits promptly stole the limelight on the underground party scene . Those in Bowery 's orbit -- regulars at London 's famed Blitz club -- must wait until later in the year to get their own moment of cultural attention in a Design Museum show dedicated to the nightclub . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> The equally bold and alarming artist Jenny Saville will be showcased in her first major British exhibition , The Anatomy of Painting , at the National Portrait Gallery from June . Saville 's unconventional portraits focus on startling ways of seeing the body , much like Bowery 's images . The exhibition will look at the lavish style of the ill-fated French monarch and her role as an emblem of unbounded excess . <p> Publishing has its own exhibitionist moment coming up in celebrating the fictional extravagance of Jay Gatsby , F Scott Fitzgerald 's enigmatic antihero of The Great Gatsby , now 100 years old . An American literary landmark , the novel will be four months into its centenary when a Tony Award-winning hit musical based on the book opens at the London Coliseum . The New Age of Sexism will tackle the swift feminisation of our obedient smart-speaker " servants " and examine how deepfake technology and virtual girlfriends all pose new threats to real women everywhere . <p> Showbiz , of course , has already embraced the digital future , and so the race is on to roll out the next convincing hologram or avatar stage show . The mega-success of Abba Voyage , revealed earlier this month to have contributed ? 1.4bn to the UK economy , has increased efforts to create another attraction . Pophouse , the Swedish firm behind Voyage , has pushed Presley rights owners to collaborate on an Elvis spectacular and has already bought up the back catalogues of glam rock band Kiss and 80s star Cyndi Lauper . Elsewhere , commercial negotiations are under way to set up an event based on David Bowie 's live shows , with the formal trademarking of a brand that includes rights to an avatar of the star . So watch this Space Oddity . Vanessa Thorpe <h> Sport <p> While there are no Olympic Games or World Cups to look forward to in 2025 , there is still plenty of big sport to whet the appetite -- led by England 's women football team defending their European title in the summer . <p> ADVERTISEMENT <p> A record 17.4 million people watched Sarina Wiegman 's side lift the Euro 2022 trophy with a 2-1 ? victory over Germany , and three years on they are among the favourites for the tournament , which takes place in Switzerland from 2 to 27 July . <p> World champions Spain look like the ones to beat , however , with France and Germany also capable of going all the way . <p> The US will also host the hugely controversial football Club World Championships on 15 June . True , people have been wearing Apple and Garmin watches for a while to record their data while exercising . " Sean Ingle <h> Film <p> Concrete provides the foundations for some of 2025 's most intriguing films . January sees the release of Architecton , a dazzling documentary by visionary Russian filmmaker Victor Kossakovsky which explores humanity 's relationship with our environment through the medium of , you 've guessed it , ? concrete . The ubiquitous grey stuff also takes a starring role alongside Adrien Brody in Brady Corbet 's Oscar-tipped The Brutalist , the sweeping , epic story of a mid-20th-century architect who flees the Nazis and finds a wealthy but demanding patron in the US . Finally , there 's the wonderfully weird Canadian comedy Universal Language , set in an alternative Persian-speaking version of Winnipeg -- a city that , according to the film 's quirky vision , is almost entirely built of concrete . <p> Fans of gothic horror will have plenty to sink their teeth into ( pun entirely intended ) in 2025 , starting with the release of Robert Eggers 's remake of the vampire classic Nosferatu on the very first day of the year . The film , which stars Lily-Rose Depp , is gloriously creepy and a sumptuously sensual visual spectacle . Mexican director Guillermo Del Toro ( Pan 's Labyrinth ) has teamed with Netflix to bring his vision of Mary Shelley 's Frankenstein to the screen . The cast includes Oscar Isaac as Dr Frankenstein and Jacob Elordi in the role of the Monster . <p> Animation is n't just for kids this year , with some of the most anticipated animated features exploring adult themes . Take Memoir of a Snail ( out in February ) from Australian Oscar-winner Adam Elliot . The film deals with depression , bad marriages , compulsive eating and hoarding , all tied together with Elliot 's trademark mordant humour . Gints Zilbalodis 's Flow , a dialogue-free animation from Latvia , explores a climate emergency through the eyes of the animals that find their world destroyed . Finally , there 's Wildwood , the latest from Laika , the studio behind Coraline . Wildwood looks set to reprise the same winning formula : like Coraline , the film is described as a " stop-motion fantasy horror " . Wendy Ide <h> Money <p> It looks as if 2025 will be a pricier year for UK consumers than anticipated . That is partly because many experts and policymakers agree that Rachel Reeves 's budget package unveiled at the end of October will push up inflation . <p> Dozens of retailers , including Tesco , Sainsbury 's and Marks &amp; Spencer , have warned that higher prices in shops are a nailed-on certainty because , they say , of the decision to boost the national living wage and raise billions of pounds by increasing employer national insurance contributions from April 2025 . <p> Meanwhile , Britons face slightly higher energy bills in January , putting more pressure on household finances , despite earlier hopes that prices would fall back . The Ofgem energy price cap for the period 1 January to 31 March 2025 has been set at ? 1,738 a year for the average dual-fuel bill -- up from the current ? 1,717 a year . <p> However , some consumers look set to receive cash windfalls that could help with the cost of living or go towards a deposit on a house , financing a big trip or paying off debts . We have all heard of " the bank of Mum and Dad " , but 2025 could be the year that " the bank of Grandma and Grandad " also starts dishing out cash in a big way . <p> This relates to an announcement in the budget that unspent money left in a pension plan after your death will be included in inheritance tax calculations from April 2027 . Experts have predicted that , as a result , many well-off older people will increasingly pass on money to grandkids , children and other family members while they are still alive ( known as giving a " living inheritance " ) . <p> They are also likely to withdraw more of their pension cash and spend it in order to reduce the value of their estate . That could make 2025 a good year for companies specialising in cruises , long-haul trips and home improvements . <p> Talking of windfalls , during the coming months we will hear more about the billions of pounds of compensation that could be paid to consumers because of an unfolding scandal involving the alleged large-scale mis-selling of car finance deals . The UK 's main financial regulator is due to provide an update in May . <p> Yet another budget announcement could mean that 2025 is a bit of a topsy-turvy year when it comes to housing market activity . Nationwide building society has predicted that the chancellor 's decision not to extend temporary stamp duty thresholds put in place by the previous government will lead to a " jump " in property sales in the first three months of 2025 , especially in March , as buyers rush to complete deals , then a " period of weakness " for the next three to six months . <p> Meanwhile , as with Taylor Swift 's shows , we can expect a flurry of news reports as analysts speculate on the scale of the spending bonanza that next summer 's Oasis reunion concerts are set to unleash . <p> The reunited Gallagher brothers are playing 17 sold-out shows in UK stadiums and parks between 4 July and 28 September ( more dates could be added ) , so that 's a lot of pints , parkas and bucket hats on top of spending on food , travel , accommodation and merch . One economic consultancy has predicted that each fan will spend ? 406 , thereby boosting the economy by almost ? 500m . Rupert Jones <h> Environment <p> One small step for Trump . One giant leap backwards for humankind . Brace yourself for a flurry of grim environmental news when the climate-denying businessman returns to the White House in January . <p> As was the case last time around , Trump is likely to kick off his administration with a series of decrees that roll back many of the nature protections and renewable energy incentives of the Biden years , particularly the Inflation Reduction Act -- the most ambitious US climate plan in history . <p> Globally , the biggest impact will be felt when Trump pulls the US out of the Paris climate agreement . The new president 's appointments will include Chris Wright , a fossil fuel executive , as energy secretary and Lee Zeldin , a former congressman who voted against wildlife refuges and oil drilling moratoriums , as head of the Environmental Protection Agency . They will be charged with promoting an " America First " agenda , which means taking a wrecking ball to any regulation that holds back fossil fuel interests and extractive industries -- and unlike during Trump 's first term , they will face fewer legal and legislative hurdles because the Republican party controls both houses and Trump appointees dominate the supreme court . <p> Renewable energy may well weather the storm because wind and solar prices are now cheaper than oil , gas and coal . The biggest impacts will be on nature , people in the global south and international efforts to tackle the climate crisis . Rightwing parties throughout the world are likely to be emboldened to step up their campaigns against net zero targets . <p> Political denials will make no difference , however , to the physics of the climate crisis , which will grow worse as long as emissions continue to rise . <p> Expect another year of supercharged extreme weather and more intense drought , fire , flooding and storms . As usual , this is likely to be felt most strongly in the northern hemisphere summer . After two years of record global heat , the expected arrival of cooling La Ni ? a conditions would normally be expected to bring some respite . But nobody is betting on that , because the world 's ? climate is now so disrupted by human activity that past patterns are no longer a reliable guide to future outcomes . If next year is another record hot year , it would be an extremely worrying sign and push fragile ecosystems , such as polar ice sheets and the Amazon rainforest , closer to a calamitous tipping point . <p> The world 's attention will be on the latter in November , when the Brazilian city of Bel ? m hosts the first ever UN climate summit in the Amazon . President Luiz In ? cio Lula da Silva has called this conference -- Cop30 -- " our last chance to avoid an irreversible collapse of the climate system " . <p> This ought to be the moment when all the countries of the world submit updated national climate plans that respond to the growing severity of the situation . But the gathering will start under a cloud because of doubts about future US participation , the hostility to the process of Argentina 's president , Javier Milei , and the host nation 's internal contradictions when it comes to nature and climate . <p> On one hand , there are extremely progressive forces inside the Brazilian government , such as environment minister Marina Silva and Indigenous minister S ? nia Guajajara -- but on the other is the powerful agribusiness and mining lobby , which dominates congress . Bel ? m will struggle to cope logistically with the tens of thousands of Cop visitors . It may have even greater trouble preventing the system of global climate governance from straining beyond breaking point . Jonathan Watts <h> Politics <p> If 2024 delivered a landslide victory and a return to power for Labour , 2025 has to be the year in which signs of national recovery become visible : the party has to show its reason for governing . <p> Keir Starmer and his party can afford to be unpopular at this point in the political cycle , even to be seen as error-prone in their first months in power . Tony Blair , after all , had difficulties after May 1997 and went on to win two more elections . <p> What Starmer 's Labour can not do , however , is continue to be perceived so negatively for much longer . <p> The omens are not good . Labour put most of its eggs in the economic growth basket in its election campaign . Starmer promised to deliver the highest growth in the G7 by the end of this parliament -- an almighty hostage to fortune . <p> Rachel Reeves 's October budget then hammered employers by raising their national insurance to repair damage done to the public finances by 14 years of Tory rule . The result , the Bank of England says , is that growth is now all but nonexistent . Reeves will explain next month how she plans to kickstart economic activity . <p> Public services , the NHS , social care , education , the courts -- all desperately need more investment so that people can feel improvement . But an economy heading in the wrong direction means tax revenues will be below expectations , giving less to spend in areas of need . <p> Dangers loom everywhere . Donald Trump 's return as US president threatens a global trade war , with tariffs of 20% on UK imports into the US , and 60% ones on those from China . The UK remains outside the EU 's single market and customs union -- so it is horribly exposed . 2025 will see preparations laid for a renegotiation of the post-Brexit trade and cooperation agreement ( TCA ) with the EU in 2026 . But Brussels is not keen on big changes , and Starmer 's government does not want to risk an overtly pro-EU stance that might boost Nigel Farage and Reform UK or benefit Kemi Badenoch 's chances of establishing herself more firmly as Tory party leader . The only move that would make a big difference -- UK re-entry into the EU single market -- will not happen in Labour 's first term . In many ways the government 's economic and political requirements are at loggerheads as Reform UK climbs in the polls . <p> Abroad , the UK needs to chart a difficult course with Trump 's Washington , the EU and China , and seek progress -- showing UK influence -- on intractable conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine . <p> A road ahead for Starmer 's government at home is not easy to see . It needs visible successes on the economy and on immigration too . <p> But with growth scraping along the bottom , evidence of improvement to living standards is likely to feel incremental at best . Labour 's best hope is to demonstrate that it has something approaching a coherent plan and that it might just be competent enough to deliver it . After medicinal treatment , doctors can recommend a procedure to remove the prostate to prevent future blockages , he said . <p> In Mr Netanyahu 's case , because the prostate is not cancerous , Dr Golan said doctors will probably perform endoscopic surgery , which is carried out by inserting small instruments into a body cavity , rather than making any surgical cuts in the abdomen . <p> The procedure lasts about an hour , Dr Golan said , and recovery is quick . <p> He added that , apart from the use of a catheter for one to three days after the procedure , patients can return to normal activity without any significant limitations . <p> Mr Netanyahu insists he is in excellent health and his office has worked to craft a public image that backs that up . @@119407325 <p> Former President Jimmy Carter , a Georgia peanut farmer who vowed to restore morality and truth to politics after an era of White House scandal and who redefined post-presidential service , died Sunday at the age of 100 . <p> The Carter Center said the 39th president died in Plains , Georgia , surrounded by his family . <p> Carter had been in home hospice care since February 2023 after a series of short hospital stays . <p> Carter , a Democrat , served a single term from 1977 to 1981 , losing a reelection bid to Ronald Reagan . Despite his notable achievements as a peacemaker , Carter 's presidency is largely remembered as an unfulfilled four years shaken by blows to America 's economy and standing overseas . His most enduring legacy , though , might be as a globetrotting elder statesman and human rights pioneer during an indefatigable 43-year " retirement . " <p> President Joe Biden said in a statement that " America and the world lost an extraordinary leader , statesman and humanitarian " as well as a man of " great character and courage , hope and optimism . " <p> " With his compassion and moral clarity , he worked to eradicate disease , forge peace , advance civil rights and human rights , promote free and fair elections , house the homeless , and always advocate for the least among us . He saved , lifted , and changed the lives of people all across the globe , " Biden said , and officially ordered a state funeral to be held in Washington , DC . <p> President-elect Donald Trump urged everyone to keep the Carter family in their prayers . " Those of us who have been fortunate to have served as President understand this is a very exclusive club , and only we can relate to the enormous responsibility of leading the Greatest Nation in History , " Trump wrote on Truth Social . " The challenges Jimmy faced as President came at a pivotal time for our country and he did everything in his power to improve the lives of all Americans . For that , we all owe him a debt of gratitude . " <p> Carter 's beloved wife , Rosalynn , died in November 2023 . They had been inseparable during their 77-year marriage , and after she passed away , the former president said in a statement that " as long as Rosalynn was in the world , I always knew somebody loved and supported me . " <p> The former president attended his wife 's memorial events , including a private burial and a televised tribute service in Atlanta , where he was seated in the front row in a reclined wheelchair . He did not deliver any remarks . <p> Carter took office in 1977 with the earnest promise to lead a government as " good and honest and decent and compassionate and filled with love as are the American people " following what had started as an unlikely long-shot bid for the Democratic Party 's nomination . <p> The Southerner with a flashing smile did enjoy significant successes , particularly abroad . He forged a rare , enduring Middle East peace deal between Israel and Egypt that stands to this day , formalized President Richard Nixon 's opening to communist China and put human rights at the center of US foreign policy . <p> But Carter was ultimately felled by a 444-day hostage crisis in Iran , in which revolutionary students flouted the US superpower by holding dozens of Americans in Tehran . The feeling of US malaise triggered by the crisis was exacerbated by Carter 's domestic struggles , including a sluggish economy , inflation and an energy crisis . <p> At times , Carter 's principled moral tone and determination to strip the presidency of ostentation , such as by selling the official yacht , Sequoia , seemed to verge on sanctimony . But out of office , Carter won admiration by living his values . Just a day after one of several falls he suffered in 2019 , he was back out building homes for Habitat for Humanity , even with an ugly black eye and 14 stitches -- and teaching Sunday school as he had done several hundreds of times . <p> The devout Southern Baptist 's life 's work was only just beginning when he limped out of the White House , humiliated by Reagan 's 1980 Republican landslide , in which the incumbent won only six states and the District of Columbia . <p> " As one of the youngest of former presidents , I expected to have many useful years ahead of me , " Carter wrote in his 1982 memoir , " Keeping Faith . " He proved as good as his word , going on to become a humanitarian icon , perhaps more popular outside the United States than he was at home . <p> Jimmy Carter , the 39th president of the United States , speaks in Elk City , Oklahoma , in 1979 . <p> Bettmann Archive/Getty Images <p> Carter is held by his mother , Lillian , when he was just a month old .
